1.9 Employee benefits
Short-term employee benefits
The cost of short-term employee benefits, (those payable within 12 months after the service is rendered, such as paid vacation 
leave and sick leave, bonuses, and non-monetary benefits such as medical care), are recognised in the period in which the 
service is rendered and are not discounted.
The expected cost of compensated absences is recognised as an expense as the employees render services that increase 
their entitlement or, in the case of non-accumulating absences, when the absence occurs.
The expected cost of profit sharing and bonus payments is recognised as an expense when there is a legal or constructive 
obligation to make such payments as a result of past performance.
1.10 Provisions and contingencies 
Provisions are recognised when:
• The company has a present obligation as a result of a past event;
• It is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation;
• A reliable estimate can be made of the obligation.
The amount of a provision is the present value of the expenditure expected to be required to settle the obligation.
Provisions are not recognised for future operating losses.
If an entity has a contract that is onerous, the present obligation under the contract shall be recognised and measured as a 
provision.
A contingent liability arises when:
• There is a possible obligation from past events which will only be confirmed by uncertain future events, or 
• There is a present obligation, but: 
– It is not probable that an outflow of resources will be required, or 
– The amount cannot be measured reliably 
A contingent asset arises when:
• There is a possible asset from past events 
• Its existence will be confirmed only by uncertain future events not fully within the entity’s control.
Contingent assets and contingent liabilities are not recognised.
Constructive obligations
A constructive obligation in terms of IAS 37, Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets, is one that arises not 
from a contract, legislation, or other operation of law, but from an entity’s own conduct. It exists when, through an established 
pattern of past practice, published policies, or a sufficiently specific current statement, an entity has signaled to other parties 
that it will accept certain responsibilities, and as a result has created a valid expectation that it will follow through. This is 
distinct from a legal obligation, which is enforceable as a matter of contract or statute.

--- Section D016 | original physical page 217 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
In prior periods, the existence of settlement negotiations and the conclusion of the 2022 and 2024 Settlement Agreements 
(each of which subsequently lapsed) gave rise to the recognition of a constructive obligation in respect of the Rebuilt Claim. 
The recognition of this constructive obligation did not constitute an admission of liability or a concession as to the validity or 
quantum of the Rebuilt Claim.
The constructive obligation is recognised when:
• a present obligation exists
• as a result of a past event
• it’s probable that settling the obligation will require an outflow of economic resources, and
• the amount can be reliably estimated.
Derecognition
Provisions shall be reviewed at the end of each reporting period and adjusted to reflect the current best estimate. If it is no 
longer probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation, the 
provision shall be reversed.
An outflow of resources or other event is regarded as probable if the event is more likely than not to occur. During the current 
financial year, management assessed that no present enforceable obligation exists in respect of the Rebuilt Claim, having 
regard to the lapsing of the 2022 and 2024 Settlement Agreements and all other relevant facts and circumstances. The 
provision has accordingly been derecognised.
1.11 Revenue 
Revenue includes contractual rental income, non-gross lettable area (non-GLA) income, contractual parking income, operating 
cost recovery, and other income.
Contractual rental income
Contractual rental income (including leases from non-GLA income and contractual parking) from operating leases is 
recognised on a straight-line basis over the lease term in accordance with IFRS 16: Leases.
Operating cost recoveries
Operating cost recoveries, comprising the Group’s recovery of costs for providing the tenant with services as determined 
by the lease agreement, are levied monthly in arrears. Operating cost recoveries are based on consumption and actual 
expenses incurred and are accounted for in accordance with IFRS 15.
Lease commission and tenant installation costs
The group pays lease commissions to secure certain contracts. These lease commissions are assessed to be an incremental 
cost of obtaining a contract. For lease commissions paid in relation to revenue contracts, which are for a period greater than 
one year, the lease commission is capitalised as non-current asset and amortised over the period of the revenue contract to 
which it relates.

--- Section D016 | original physical page 218 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
1.11 Revenue (cont.)
Tenant installation costs represent expenditure incurred by Accelerate in preparing leased premises for occupation by 
tenants. Where such costs meet the recognition criteria of an asset — that is, it is probable that future economic benefits will 
flow to the entity and the cost can be measured reliably — they are capitalised and classified as part of investment property. 
Capitalised tenant installation costs are amortised on a straight-line basis over the lease term.
Other rental income
Other income, which includes parking income, is recognised in the accounting period in which control of the services is 
passed to the customer, which is when the service is rendered. For certain service contracts, revenue is recognised based on 
the actual service provided to the end of the reporting period as a proportion of the total services to be provided because the 
customer receives and uses the benefits simultaneously.
1.12 Other accounting policies
Property acquisitions and business combinations
Where property is acquired, via corporate acquisitions or otherwise, management considers the substance of the assets and 
activities of the acquired entity in determining whether the acquisition represents the acquisition of a business as per IFRS 3. 
Where such acquisitions are not judged to be acquisitions of a business, they are not treated as business combinations. 
Rather, the cost to acquire the corporate entity is allocated between the identifiable assets and liabilities of the entity based 
on their relative fair values at the acquisition date. Accordingly, no goodwill or additional deferred taxation arises. Otherwise, 
acquisitions are accounted for as business combinations.
Investment property acquisitions which do not meet the definition of a business as defined in IFRS 3 are recognised and 
measured in accordance with IAS 40.
Cash and cash equivalents
Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash on hand, demand deposits and other short-term highly liquid investments that are 
readily convertible to a known amount of cash and are subject to an insignificant risk of change in value. These are initially 
recorded at fair value and subsequently recorded at amortised cost.
Bank overdraft and borrowings
Bank overdrafts and borrowings are initially measured at fair value less directly attributable transaction costs and are 
subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective interest rate method.
Tenant deposits
Tenant deposit liabilities are initially recognised at fair value and subsequently measured at amortised cost where the effect 
of discounting is material. Any difference between the initial fair value and the nominal amount is included as a component 
of operating lease income and recognised on a straight-line basis over the lease term.

--- Section D016 | original physical page 219 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
Insurance Proceeds
Insurance proceeds are recognised when Accelerate established a right to receive compensation, which is when it is virtually 
certain that the insurer will accept the claim. Proceeds are not offset against the related loss or expenditure but are recognised 
separately in other income in profit or loss.
Finance income
Finance income is recognised as it accrues using the effective interest rate (EIR) method. EIR is the rate that exactly discounts 
the estimated future cash payments or receipts over the expected life of the financial instrument or a shorter period, where 
appropriate, to the net carrying amount of the financial asset or liability. Finance income is included in finance income in the 
statement of comprehensive income.
Current income tax
Current tax liabilities/(assets) for the current and prior periods are measured at the amount expected to be paid to/(recovered 
from) the tax authorities, using the tax rates and tax laws that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the 
reporting period.
Accelerate is registered as a REIT, and as such will only pay tax on profits not distributed to shareholders as set out in the 
Income Tax Act of 1962 section 25BB.
Current tax for current and prior periods is, to the extent unpaid, recognised as a liability. If the amount already paid in 
respect of current and prior periods exceeds the amount due for those periods, the excess is recognised as an asset.
Taxes
Accelerate converted to a Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) on listing. As a result, section 25BB of the Income Tax Act 
applies to qualifying REIT income and expenses. The legislation provides that capital gains on sale of investment properties 
are not taxable and previous building allowances claimed will be recouped at 27%. All rental income and dividends from 
property subsidiaries will be taxed at 27% and any qualifying distribution paid from these taxable profits will be deductible at 
27%. Should the entities’ assets be sold, or the entity wound up, there could be a tax liability to the value of the recoupments 
previously claimed.
Accelerate is of the view that the provisions of IAS 12 Income Taxes regarding different tax rates for distributed and 
undistributed profits are intended to apply where the only significant factor determining the differential tax rate is the 
retention or distribution of profit. This view is applied given that this would reflect the economic reality of Accelerate as being 
tax neutral and would not result in deferred taxation being raised at each reporting date merely to be reversed after the end 
of the reporting date when distributions are declared to shareholders. 
The entity can choose to operate within one of two tax regimes, either a ‘full tax’ regime by not distributing rental income 
and dividends from property subsidiaries to shareholders or a ‘no tax’ regime by distributing rental income and dividends 
from property subsidiaries to shareholders, rather than operating in a single tax regime with a dual tax rate, depending 
on whether profits are retained or distributed. Accordingly, the measurement of deferred tax assets and liabilities takes 
into account expected future distributions. This results in no deferred tax being recognised by Accelerate on REIT assets 
and liabilities

--- Section D017 | original physical page 220 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
1.12 Other accounting policies (cont.)
Current taxes are recognised as income or expense and included in profit or loss for the period, except to the extent that the 
tax arises from:
• A transaction or event which is recognised, in the same or different period, to other comprehensive income; or
• A business combination.
Current tax and deferred taxes are charged or credited to other comprehensive income if the tax relates to items that are 
credited or charged, in the same or different period, to other comprehensive income.
Current tax and deferred taxes are charged or credited directly to equity if the tax relates to items that are credited or 
charged, in the same or different period, directly to equity.
Share capital
Ordinary shares are classified as equity. Accelerate shares held by Accelerate Treasury Proprietary Limited are classified as 
treasury shares on consolidation and presented as a deduction from equity and these shares are held at cost.
Fair value measurements
Accelerate measures certain financial instruments such as derivatives, and non-financial assets such as investment property, 
at fair value at the end of each reporting period. For financial instruments measured at amortised cost, the fair values are 
also disclosed in the financial statements when the carrying values are not determined to approximate fair value.
Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between 
market participants at the measurement date. The fair value measurement is based on the presumption that the transaction 
to sell the asset or transfer the liability takes place either:
• In the principal market for the asset or liability; or
• In the absence of a principal market, in the most advantageous market for the asset or liability. Accelerate must be able 
to access the principal or the most advantageous market at the measurement date.
The fair value of an asset or a liability is measured using the assumptions market participants would use when pricing the 
asset or liability, assuming that market participants act in their economic best interest.
A fair value measurement of a non-financial asset takes into account a market participant’s ability to generate economic 
benefits by using the asset in its highest and best use or by selling it to another market participant that would use the asset 
in its highest and best use.
Accelerate uses valuation techniques that are appropriate in the circumstances and for which sufficient data is available 
to measure fair value, maximising the use of relevant observable inputs and minimising the use of unobservable inputs 
significant to the fair value measurement as a whole

--- Section D017 | original physical page 221 | text selection | Mixed / unspecified ---
Assets and liabilities for which fair value is measured or disclosed in the financial statements are categorised within the fair 
value hierarchy, described as follows based on the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement as a 
whole:
Level 1 – Quoted (unadjusted) market prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities
Level 2 –	 Valuation techniques for which the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement is directly or 
indirectly observable
Level 3 – Valuation techniques for which the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement is unobservable.
For assets and liabilities that are recognised in the financial statements on a recurring basis, Accelerate determines whether 
transfers have occurred between levels in the hierarchy by reassessing categorisation (based on the lowest level input that is 
significant to the fair value measurement as a whole) at the end of each reporting period.
The fair value of financial instruments that are not traded in an active market (for example, over-the-counter derivatives) is 
determined by using valuation techniques. Accelerate uses a variety of methods and makes assumptions that are based on 
market conditions existing at the end of each reporting period. Quoted market prices or dealer quotes for similar instruments 
are used for long-term debt. Other techniques, such as estimated discounted cash flows, are used to determine fair value for 
the remaining financial instruments. The fair value of interest rate swaps is calculated as the present value of the estimated 
future cash flows.
The fair value of investment property is determined by using valuation techniques. Accelerate uses a variety of methods and 
makes assumptions that are based on market conditions existing at the end of each reporting period and highest and best 
use depending on valuation outcome. Techniques include discounted cash flows and capitalisation rate methods.
The carrying value of trade receivables and payables approximate their fair values.
The fair value of financial liabilities for disclosure purposes is estimated by discounting the future contractual cash flows 
at the current market interest rate that is available to Accelerate for similar financial instruments. Accelerate’s own non￾performance risk is considered.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Rebuilt Claim constructive obligation derecognition** `[D017, physical PDF p. 217]`: The policy states that in prior periods, settlement negotiations and the 2022 and 2024 Settlement Agreements (each of which subsequently lapsed) gave rise to a **constructive obligation** in respect of the Rebuilt Claim, and that recognition "did not constitute an admission of liability or a concession as to the validity or quantum." During the current year, management assessed **no present enforceable obligation exists** and the provision was **derecognised**. This is the accounting basis for the R300,000k derecognition (Q7/Q27/Q45/Q72/Q149). It confirms the item is a **non-cash reversal of a provision** — a non-distributable, FFO-excluded item. **Must verify in D018**: the exact P&L line, the R300,000k amount, and whether any residual contingent liability or contingent asset is disclosed (since contingent assets/liabilities are not recognised per p.216).

- **Insurance proceeds recognition** `[D016, physical PDF p. 219]`: "Insurance proceeds are recognised when Accelerate established a right to receive compensation, which is when it is virtually certain that the insurer will accept the claim. Proceeds are **not offset against the related loss or expenditure but are recognised separately in other income** in profit or loss." This confirms the R82,500k insurance (Q85/Q18/Q51) sits gross in other income, not netted against capex or the fire loss. **Must verify in D018**: the 50% joint-operation share basis, the R43,5m capex application, and whether the insurance is a one-off requiring FFO exclusion.

- **Derivatives — no hedge accounting** `[D016, physical PDF pp. 213–214]`: Derivatives carried at **fair value through profit or loss**, gains/losses recognised immediately in P&L; used only to hedge interest rate risk, not for trading. This confirms swap MTM is a **non-cash P&L item** (FFO add-back) and that **no hedge accounting/OCI** is applied. **Must verify in D018**: swap notional, over-hedge risk post Mar 2027, and the MTM amount (Q31/Q88/Q107).

- **Investment property fair value — Level 3, DCF and cap rate methods** `[D016, physical PDF pp. 207–208; D017, physical PDF p. 221]`: Fair value determined by real estate valuation experts and management under IFRS 13; methods include **discounted cash flows and capitalisation rate methods**; classified **Level 3** (unobservable inputs). Changes in fair value **excluded from distributable income**. **Must verify in D018 Note 2/34**: weighted average cap rate, discount rate, exit cap rate, vacancy and rental-growth assumptions per sector (Q97/Q100), and the external vs internal valuation split.

- **Held-for-sale measured at IAS 40 fair value** `[D016, physical PDF pp. 209–210]`: Held-for-sale comprises **solely investment properties**, excluded from IFRS 5 measurement scope, and **continue to be measured at IAS 40 fair value** with gains/losses in P&L. Fair value less costs to sell based on **market evidence, offers received, or independent valuations** `[D016, physical PDF p. 207]`. **Must verify in D018 Note 12**: composition of R576,800k, carrying values, transfer timing, and any held-for-sale liabilities (Q108/Q102).

- **Company investments in subsidiaries at FV through P&L** `[D016, physical PDF pp. 206–207]`: In the separate financial statements, investments in subsidiaries are carried at **fair value through profit or loss**; on disposal the difference between proceeds and fair value is recognised in P&L; fair value calculated with reference to **net asset value of underlying assets and liabilities**. This supports the Company-level investment reduction (Q105) being a fair value write-down (non-cash, FFO exclusion). **Must verify in D018**: the R312,010k investment reduction and R524,908k loans-to-group reduction split.

- **Intra-group elimination** `[D016, physical PDF p. 205]`: "All intra-Group transactions, balances and unrealised gains and losses are eliminated on consolidation." This supports the −93% collapse in Group financing income (Q119/Q141) being driven by intra-group elimination changes. **Must verify in D018 Note 24**: the R105,688k intra-group elimination and external interest source.

- **REIT tax regime — no deferred tax** `[D017, physical PDF p. 219]`: Section 25BB applies; capital gains on property sales not taxable; rental income/dividends taxed at 27% but deductible at 27% if distributed; **no deferred tax recognised on REIT assets and liabilities**. Reinforces nil tax (Q121). **Must verify in D018**: any recoupment liability disclosure on asset sale/winding-up.

- **Treasury shares** `[D017, physical PDF p. 220]`: Accelerate shares held by Accelerate Treasury Proprietary Limited classified as **treasury shares on consolidation, deducted from equity, held at cost**. Relevant to weighted average share count for FFO/NAV per share (Q89/Q110/Q120). **Must verify in D018 Note 29**: weighted average shares and treasury share count (44,829,303).

- **Tenant installation costs capitalised into investment property** `[D016, physical PDF p. 218]`: TI costs meeting asset recognition criteria are **capitalised and classified as part of investment property**, amortised straight-line over the lease term. Lease commissions capitalised as non-current asset and amortised over the revenue contract period `[D016, physical PDF p. 217]`. Relevant to capex classification (Q93/Q131) and to the Fourways Mall FV increase despite NPI fall (Q138) — capex capitalisation can lift valuation. **Must verify in D018**: TI/lease commission quantum and Fourways Mall capex capitalisation.

- **Lease modification / rent relief** `[D016, physical PDF p. 215]`: The Group elected **lease modification under IFRS 16** for reduced past lease payments; relief accounted for as a **lease incentive** recognised as a **reduction to lease income over the lease term**. Relevant to the straight-line lease accrual (R49,702k) and to Fourways Mall NPI decline (Q137) if rent relief was granted. **Must verify in D018**: rent relief quantum and straight-line accrual composition.

- **Missing footnote definitions**: The `[^co]`/`[^nt]` footnote definitions on the D016 p.202 heading are **not present** in this D016–D017 capture. The policies confirm Fourways Mall is a **joint operation** (likely "co") and refer to "non-GLA income" (likely "nt"), but the exact footnote wording is missing. **Must verify in D018/D020** (Q136).

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **`[^co][^nt].` markers on Note 2 heading** `[D018.1, pp. 228, 230]`: The footnote definitions are **NOT present in this section capture**. Per the no-fabrication rule, I explicitly state the footnote text is missing. These markers likely denote "co-owned/joint operation" and "not tested/not audited" or similar — but this must be verified in D020 (REIT Disclosures) or the D018 footnote register. **Verification question raised (Q165/Q136).**

- **Narrative qualification p. 229**: *"The increased weighted average expected rental value per m² is due to escalation as well as the reduced number of properties. The widening of the rental/m² range is similarly due to the reduction of the number of properties with the remaining assets having a wider range. This also affects the rental growth range and the weighted average capitalisation rate."* `[D018.1, p. 229]`
  - **Implication**: The apparent deterioration in WACR (Commercial 8,1%→9,4%) and rental growth range is **partly a portfolio-composition artefact**, not purely market cap-rate expansion. This is critical for forecasting: the Commercial WACR jump of +130bp is contaminated by disposal of lower-cap-rate assets, so the true like-for-like cap-rate movement is smaller. Must verify in Note 22 / D008 which commercial assets were disposed.

- **Narrative qualification p. 229**: *"The fair value adjustments on investment property (refer to note 22), which are excluded from the calculation of SA REIT funds from operations, are included in profit and loss and categorised as level 3 under the fair value hierarchy (refer to note 34)..."* `[D018.1, p. 229]`
  - **Implication for DIPS bridge**: Confirms FV adjustments are **excluded from SA REIT FFO** — a key non-distributable add-back. The R423,412k Group / R416,846k Company FV adjustment (per D012/Q116) must be added back in the FFO reconciliation. Level 3 classification confirmed (ties to Q97).

- **Narrative qualification p. 229**: *"Capital commitments are set out in note 27."* `[D018.1, p. 229]`
  - **Implication**: Forward capex/development commitments are in Note 27, not here. **New verification question raised** — extract capital commitments quantum for forecast capex line.

- **Sensitivity table arithmetic check** `[D018.1, pp. 229–230]`:
  - Cap rate +50bp: Group −R346,230k; −50bp: +R396,588k. Asymmetry (down-side larger than up-side) is normal for DCF/cap-rate convexity — no arithmetic error flagged.
  - Discount rate +50bp: Group −R180,897k; −50bp: +R188,742k — symmetric, consistent.
  - Vacancy +50bp: −R35,514k; −50bp: +R35,514k — perfectly symmetric, consistent.
  - Gross income ±1%: ±R71,028k — symmetric, consistent.
  - Property expenses ±1%: ±R23,459k — symmetric, consistent.
  - **Cross-check**: Gross income sensitivity (R71,028k) vs property expense sensitivity (R23,459k) implies expense ratio ≈ 33% of gross income — plausible for a retail-heavy portfolio. No arithmetic tension.
  - **Anomaly flagged**: Commercial discount rate decrease 2025 Group = +R166,021k vs 2026 Group = +R8,530k — a ~95% collapse in discount-rate sensitivity for Commercial, consistent with the commercial portfolio shrinking from R2,154,798k to R970,600k. Not an error, but confirms commercial disposal dominance.

- **Company vs Group Commercial discount rate sensitivity**: Company shows "N/A" for Commercial discount rate sensitivity `[D018.1, p. 229]` while Group shows R8,524k/R8,530k. This implies the Company's remaining R200,000k commercial asset is valued on a **cap-rate method only (no DCF discount rate input)**, whereas Group's R970,600k commercial includes DCF-valued assets in subsidiaries/JV. **Verification question raised** — confirm valuation method split (cap rate vs DCF) per property in Note 34.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **`[^co][^nt].` markers on Note 4 heading** [D018.2, physical PDF p. 232]: The footnote definitions are **missing from this section capture**. These markers also appeared on the Note 2 heading [D018.1 pp. 228, 230]. They likely denote "Company" and "not tested/not audited" or similar assurance-scope annotations, but this must **not** be assumed. Verification question raised (Q175/Q165) to locate exact wording in D018 remainder or D020. If `[^nt]` means "not tested," it would confirm that certain note disclosures (including Note 2 valuation inputs and Note 4 PPE) fall outside the audited scope — material for assessing reliability of the valuation inputs used in the forecast.

- **Note 3 — Straight-line rental income accrual** [D018.2, p. 230]: No footnote markers, but the table itself is a critical non-cash reconciliation item:
  - Group investment property SL accrual **reversed R36,409k** in FY2026 (vs R32,719k in FY2025) — a larger non-cash deduction from IFRS rental income than prior year, which must be **added back** in the SA REIT FFO/distributable earnings bridge.
  - Held-for-sale SL: **R13,431k released on disposal** — non-cash, must be excluded from distributable earnings and from NPI-on-disposal calculations.
  - Net Group SL movement: opening R121,572k + R23,157k (HFS) = R144,729k; closing R81,523k + R13,504k = R95,027k; net reduction **R49,702k** — this reconciles to the R49,702k figure in the stored ledger (Q160). So the R49,702k is the **net balance-sheet reduction**, not the P&L accrual. This resolves the apparent tension: P&L accrual R36,409k + R138k HFS − R13,431k disposal release = R23,116k; the difference to R49,702k is the HFS transfer to investment property (R3,640k) and other transfers. **Flag**: the arithmetic bridge from P&L accrual to balance-sheet movement needs a clean reconciliation in D020 (Q125).
  - Company SL accrual only **R212k** vs Group R36,409k — implies the bulk of straight-line accrual sits in subsidiaries, consistent with the R770,600k Group commercial FV in subsidiaries/JV (Q172).

- **Note 4 — PPE** [D018.2, pp. 231–232]: Immaterial (carrying amount R108k Group / R99k Company). No forecast impact. Note the Company IT equipment cost R930k vs Group R979k — R49k difference sits in subsidiaries; immaterial.

- **Note 5 — Right-of-use asset** [D018.2, p. 233]: ROU asset R1,746k (2025: R311k), additions R1,924k for **Cedar Square CCTV upgrade** and office printers. This implies a new lease liability of ~R1,924k (to be confirmed in the lease note). Immaterial to LTV/ICR but confirms Cedar Square remains operational and capex is being incurred there. Depreciation R489k is non-cash (added back in FFO).

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

- **Q105 (High) & Q163 (Medium): Investment in subsidiaries fell R312,010k; loans to group fell R524,908k — identify impairment/write-down vs repayment; P&L line and FFO exclusion.**
    - **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D018.4+ / D020)`
    - **Answer & evidence**: Note 6 [D018.3, p. 233] shows the carrying amount of investments in subsidiaries fell from R772,217k to R460,207k, a decrease of R312,010k. This is fully explained by the movement in the underlying net asset values of the subsidiaries, which are driven by the fair value of their investment properties (Note 2) less inter-company loans (Note 7). The decrease is therefore a fair value movement, not a cash impairment. Note 7 [D018.3, p. 236] shows the net loans to group companies *increased* from R364,379k to R408,233k. The R524,908k fall in the gross non-current loans to group balance (from R949,654k to R424,746k) is explained by a non-cash reclassification of R512,093k from non-current to current liabilities (the Wanooka loan became payable on demand), not a cash repayment. The P&L line for the investment decrease is the share of fair value adjustment in subsidiaries, which is a non-distributable item and should be excluded from SA REIT FFO. The R5,594k ECL allowance increase is a non-cash P&L charge.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 6 — Investment in Subsidiaries [D018.3, p. 233]:**
    - **Qualification**: "The fair value of the investment in subsidiaries is based on the net asset value of the subsidiary and is classified as level 3 in the fair value hierarchy. The net asset values of the subsidiaries approximate fair value."
    - **Implication**: This confirms that the R312,010k decrease in the investment carrying amount is a non-cash fair value movement, driven by the underlying property valuations (Note 2) and inter-company loans (Note 7). This is a non-distributable item and must be excluded from SA REIT FFO. The key inputs are the property valuations and loan values.

- **Note 6 — Sensitivity Analysis [D018.3, pp. 234–235]:**
    - **Qualification**: The sensitivity table shows the impact of a 50bps change in discount/cap rate on the fair value of the investment in subsidiaries. For PCP (which holds Wanooka/KPMG), a 50bps increase reduces fair value by R5,967k; for Wanooka directly, by R2,557k. For Pybus (Citibank), a 50bps increase in bulk rate *increases* fair value by R1,738k (counter-intuitive, likely due to the nature of the bulk rate input).
    - **Implication**: These sensitivities are small relative to the R460,207k carrying amount, suggesting the subsidiary valuations are not highly sensitive to cap rate changes. This is a non-cash item for FFO purposes.

- **Note 7 — Loans To/(From) Group Companies [D018.3, pp. 236–237]:**
    - **Qualification**: "The loans to group companies (except for the loan to Accelerate Treasury Proprietary Limited) bear interest at a rate of 9,87% (2025: 11,15%) per annum linked to JIBAR... The Company will transition to ZARONIA as the applicable reference rate upon the cessation of JIBAR in December 2026."
    - **Implication**: This is a critical forward-looking disclosure. The transition from JIBAR to ZARONIA in December 2026 creates a potential interest rate basis risk. The 9.87% rate is the Company's cost of funding on-lent to subsidiaries. The ECL allowance of R280,849k (2025: R286,443k) is a non-cash item. The R5,594k increase in ECL is a P&L charge that should be added back in FFO.
    - **Qualification**: "The loans to APF Treasury and Pybus Sixty-Two (RF) Proprietary Limited are both subordinated until these companies meet solvency and liquidity requirements... The loans have no fixed repayment terms and are repayable on demand."
    - **Implication**: The subordination of the Pybus loan (R418,236k) is a significant risk factor. If Pybus (which holds the Citibank building) cannot meet its solvency/liquidity requirements, the loan may not be recoverable. The ECL allowance on Pybus is only R1,619k, which appears low relative to the R418,236k exposure. This is a key verification point.

- **Note 8 — Joint Operation [D018.3, p. 237]:**
    - **Qualification**: "Accelerate owns 50% of Fourways Mall through an undivided share. Investment property relating to the Fourways Mall retail site recognised in the financial statements of Accelerate amounts to R4,2 billion (2025: R4,0 billion)... The remaining 50% of Fourways Mall is owned by Azrapart Proprietary Limited. Azrapart was placed in business rescue. Accelerate and the Business Rescue Practitioner continue to make joint decisions for the Joint operation."
    - **Implication**: This is the most consequential disclosure in this section. The 50% co-owner is in business rescue, meaning Accelerate has joint control with a Business Rescue Practitioner. This creates governance and decision-making risk. The investment property value of R4,228,800k is a key component of the Group's R6,600,000k portfolio. The NPI collapse (R201,766k → R121,743k) and the receivables collapse (R545,806k → R94,428k) are critical drivers of the group's financial performance and the related-party write-off.
    - **Qualification**: "Currently Fourways Mall is being managed by Flanagan and Gerard and the Moolman Group as the Asset and Property Manager."
    - **Implication**: This confirms the management arrangement but does not disclose the fee/profit-share terms. This is a related-party disclosure gap.

10. Trade and Other Receivables (cont.)                                   
* Vendor loans, previously fully impaired has been written off however, recovery of the amounts due will continue.
** Related party receivable has been written off however, recovery of the amounts due will continue.
                                                                          
# The Headlease was an agreement entered into between the Company and FWP in which FWP guaranteed certain rentals for vacant space for a
period of three years post the redevelopment of the enlarged Fourways Mall.
## No expected credit loss allowance has been recognised on the related party receivable. The balance is expected to be settled in full and
management has therefore assessed the probability of default and resulting expected credit losses as immaterial.
                                                                          
                                                                          
All amounts are short term. The net carrying amount of trade and other receivables is considered a reasonable
approximation of fair value. The Group applies the IFRS 9 simplified approach to measuring expected credit losses using a
lifetime expected credit loss provision for trade receivables. To measure expected credit losses on an individual basis, trade
receivables are assessed net of deposit or guarantee held. Arrears aged 90 days and over are in most instances deemed
to be irrecoverable and provided for. The expected loss rates are based on the Group’s historical credit losses experienced
                                                                          
over a period of 36 months prior to the period end and are reassessed at each reporting date.
                                                                          
In July 2024, the Company and Mr Georgiou (on behalf of the Related Parties) signed a Settlement Agreement which would
have resulted in the settlement of amounts due from various entities (approximately R970 ,7 million) to the Company. Firstly,
the debt from the various entities would have been ceded and assigned to Azrapart whereafter, the amount of Azrapart’s
claim (R300,0 million) would be set off against the debt due to the Company. Thereafter, further assets (in the form of
bulk and parking) would have been acquired from Azrapart with the termination amounts for the property management
companies (FWP and APMC) also being set-off against the debt due to the Company. The Settlement Agreement would
                                                                          
have resulted in a net settlement of amounts due and payable with no outflow of cash for the Company.
                                                                          
The Settlement Agreement however lapsed during November 2024 as certain suspensive conditions were not met.
Management engaged in further negotiations with Azrapart with a view to resolving outstanding matters. No new
agreement was concluded and the receivables due to the Company from the Related Parties were fully impaired at the
prior year end.                                                           
                                                                          
In the current financial year, the outstanding amounts due from the Related Party were written off. Despite the write off,
the Company will continue to seek recovery of amounts due from the Related Parties. The Company does not accept the
validity of the Rebuilt Claim asserted by Azrapart and maintains that no present enforceable obligation exists in respect
thereof.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `*` — Vendor loans [D018.4, physical PDF p. 240]:**
"Vendor loans, previously fully impaired has been written off however, recovery of the amounts due will continue."
- **What it changes**: The R59,489k vendor loan balance was fully impaired in prior years (ECL R59,489k) and is now written off against the ECL allowance (R59,489k write-off in the ECL movement). This is a non-cash derecognition — no P&L impact in FY2026 (the impairment was already taken). Recovery efforts continue, implying a potential contingent asset not recognised on balance sheet. **FFO treatment**: no FY2026 P&L impact, so no FFO adjustment needed for the write-off itself; but any future recovery would be a non-distributable gain (should be excluded from FFO). Verification: confirm no FY2026 P&L line for vendor loan write-off and check contingent asset disclosure.

**Footnote `**` — Related party receivable [D018.4, physical PDF p. 240]:**
"Related party receivable has been written off however, recovery of the amounts due will continue."
- **What it changes**: The R430,095k related-party receivable was fully impaired in prior years (ECL R430,095k) and is now written off against the ECL allowance. Non-cash derecognition — no FY2026 P&L impact. Recovery efforts continue. **FFO treatment**: no FY2026 P&L impact; future recovery would be non-distributable. Verification: confirm the R430,095k is the carrying amount written off (not the R970,7m gross exposure) and that the R300,0m Rebuilt Claim derecognition is a separate liability release (P&L line still unidentified).

**Footnote `#` — Headlease [D018.4, physical PDF p. 240]:**
"The Headlease was an agreement entered into between the Company and FWP in which FWP guaranteed certain rentals for vacant space for a period of three years post the redevelopment of the enlarged Fourways Mall."
- **What it changes**: The R540,611k headlease receivable was a guarantee from FWP (related party) for vacant space rentals post-Fourways Mall redevelopment. It was fully impaired in prior years (ECL R540,611k) and written off in FY2026. This is a **related-party guarantee that failed** — FWP is the former property manager. The write-off confirms the guarantee is not recoverable. **FFO treatment**: non-cash, no FY2026 P&L impact. Verification: confirm FWP's related-party status post-Georgiou retirement (Q90) and whether any claim against FWP remains (contingent asset).

**Footnote `##` — Other receivables at amortised cost [D018.4, physical PDF p. 240]:**
"No expected credit loss allowance has been recognised on the related party receivable. The balance is expected to be settled in full and management has therefore assessed the probability of default and resulting expected credit losses as immaterial."
- **What it changes**: **This is the most consequential footnote in the section and contains an apparent labelling inconsistency.** The `##` marker sits on "Other receivables at amortised cost" (R56,130k, 2025: nil), but the footnote text refers to "the related party receivable." Two possibilities: (a) the R56,130k "Other receivables" is itself a related-party receivable (new in FY2026) and management has assessed it as fully recoverable; or (b) the footnote is mis-labelled and should attach to a different line. Given the R430,095k related-party receivable was written off, the R56,130k cannot be the same balance. **This requires urgent verification** — if the R56,130k is a new related-party receivable with no ECL, it is a significant judgment that could reverse in FY2027. **FFO treatment**: no ECL charge in FY2026, so no FFO adjustment; but if the balance is impaired in FY2027, it would be a non-cash FFO add-back. Verification question Q193 below.

**Settlement Agreement narrative [D018.4, physical PDF p. 240]:**
- **What it changes**: The July 2024 Settlement Agreement with Mr Georgiou (on behalf of Related Parties) would have settled ~R970,7m via: (i) cession of debt to Azrapart; (ii) set-off of Azrapart's R300,0m Rebuilt Claim; (iii) acquisition of bulk and parking from Azrapart; (iv) set-off of FWP/APMC termination amounts. **The agreement lapsed November 2024** as suspensive conditions were not met. No new agreement concluded. Receivables fully impaired at prior year end and written off in FY2026. Company "does not accept the validity of the Rebuilt Claim asserted by Azrapart and maintains that no present enforceable obligation exists in respect thereof."
- **Implications**: (1) The R970,7m gross exposure is **not** the carrying amount written off — the carrying amount was R430,095k (related party) + R540,611k (headlease) + R59,489k (vendor loans) = R1,030,195k, of which R1,116,632k total write-off includes trade receivable ECL movements. (2) The R300,0m Rebuilt Claim is **not recognised as a liability** — the Company disputes it. This is a contingent liability at most. (3) The failed settlement means the related-party dispute is unresolved and recovery efforts continue — potential contingent asset. (4) **FFO treatment**: the write-offs are non-cash and should be added back in the SA REIT FFO bridge; the R300,0m derecognition (if it was a liability release) should be excluded from FFO as non-distributable.

**ECL policy qualification [D018.4, physical PDF p. 240]:**
"Arrears aged 90 days and over are in most instances deemed to be irrecoverable and provided for. The expected loss rates are based on the Group's historical credit losses experienced over a period of 36 months prior to the period end and are reassessed at each reporting date."
- **What it changes**: The 36-month historical loss rate basis is a simplified approach. Given the FY2025 related-party write-off of R998,961k (per ECL movement: opening R124,502k, increase R998,961k, closing R1,123,463k), the historical loss experience is now dominated by the related-party default — this may overstate future ECL on trade receivables. Verification: confirm the FY2027 ECL rate assumption and whether the 36-month window will still include the FY2025 related-party default.

**Cash note qualification [D018.4, physical PDF p. 241]:**
"None of the cash balances for the current financial year are encumbered due to bank guarantees lodged for municipal and other deposits (2025: R9,4 million)."
- **What it changes**: All R110,456k cash is unrestricted in FY2026 (vs R9,4m encumbered in FY2025). This improves liquidity headroom but the R102,544k YoY increase is largely disposal proceeds held (links Q127/Q129). Verification: confirm the cash is genuinely available (not held in a disposal escrow) and that the R70,4m undrawn facilities are committed.

**JIBAR transition qualification [D018.4, physical PDF p. 238]:**
"The Group will transition from JIBAR-linked instruments to ZARONIA-linked instruments in December 2026... The Group does not expect the IBOR reform to have a material impact on its financial position or performance."
- **What it changes**: The R3,002.0m debt, R5.5m derivatives and R424.7m group loans all reference JIBAR and will transition before 31 Dec 2026. The "no material impact" assertion is management's view — verification required on basis risk and swap MTM reclassification. **FFO treatment**: any transition-related swap MTM movement would be non-cash and should be excluded from FFO.

valued at financial year-end in terms of IAS 40. The fair value adjustments on investment property, which are excluded
from the calculation of distributable earnings, are included in profit and loss and categorised as level 3 under the fair value
hierarchy in note 34 based on the inputs to the valuation technique used.
The directors are committed to the disposal of non-current assets held-for-sale and envisage conclusion of sale agreements
within 12 months following financial year-end. The requirements of IFRS 5 have been met in appropriately classifying these
assets as held-for-sale.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `*` [D018.5, p. 242] — "Represents the fair value difference between the sale price and the market value pre-disposal."**
- The movement table shows "Disposals (788,500)" then "Fair value included in disposal* (8,558)" giving "Net disposal value (779,942)". This means the R788,500k gross selling price includes R8,558k that had already been recognised as fair value uplift pre-classification; the carrying value removed from held-for-sale is therefore R779,942k. **Implication for forecast**: the profit/loss on disposal in the income statement is *not* R788,500k less carrying value — the R8,558k is a reclassification, not a new gain. Must verify in Note 22 / income statement that the disposal gain line excludes this R8,558k to avoid double-counting in FFO/distributable earnings.

**Footnote `*` [D018.5, p. 244] — sale-agreement valuations.**
- Five of eight FY2026 held-for-sale properties (Beacon Isle, Valleyview, The Buzz Shopping Centre, The Buzz vacant land, Waterford) are valued at **sale-agreement prices**, not DCF. These are excluded from the weighted-average cap rate (9.75%), rental growth (6.0%), vacancy (5.0%) and sensitivity disclosures. **Implication**: the R576,800k held-for-sale valuation is largely contractually locked, so downside fair-value risk on these five is low — but the R135,000k Oceana House + R65,000k Thomas Pattullo (the two commercial DCF-valued assets) carry the sensitivity. The commercial sensitivity table [p. 245] shows ±50bp cap rate = −R9,756k / +R10,811k; ±50bp discount rate = −R3,900k / +R4,000k; ±50bp vacancy = ∓R1,700k; ±1% gross income = ±R3,401k; ±1% property expenses = ∓R1,139k. These sensitivities apply **only to the two DCF-valued commercial assets** (Oceana House + Thomas Pattullo = R200,000k), not the full R576,800k — a critical distinction for forecasting fair-value volatility.

**Footnote `#` [D018.5, pp. 244–245] — prior-year basis.**
- FY2025: eight disposal assets valued on sale agreements (no sensitivities); remaining three valued on **cap rate valuation** (not DCF). FY2026 switched to DCF for the three non-sale-agreement assets. **Implication**: year-on-year cap rate comparison (9.20% → 9.75%) is not like-for-like — methodology changed. Flag for Q100/Q151.

**Qualification [D018.5, p. 245] — "Non-current assets held-for-sale have been pledged as security for interest-bearing borrowings per note 2."**
- The R576,800k held-for-sale portfolio is **encumbered**. This matters for LTV and disposal proceeds: proceeds must first settle secured debt before any surplus is available. Must verify in Note 2/23 which facilities are secured against these assets and whether disposal proceeds are ring-fenced.

**Qualification [D018.5, p. 245] — "fair value adjustments … excluded from the calculation of distributable earnings … categorised as level 3."**
- Confirms the R27,965k FY2026 held-for-sale fair value adjustment (2025: R3,774k) is **non-distributable** — exclude from DIPS/FFO. Also confirms Level 3 classification for Note 34.

**Qualification [D018.5, p. 245] — "directors … envisage conclusion of sale agreements within 12 months following financial year-end."**
- Forward-looking commitment. If sale agreements are not concluded within 12 months, IFRS 5 classification may need reversal and assets reclassified to investment property — a forecast risk. Must check post-year-end disposal announcements in D020 / SENS.

**Footnote [D018.5, p. 247] — lease liabilities.**
- "The Group is not potentially exposed to future cash outflows not reflected in the measurement of the lease liability." Confirms no variable lease payments, no extension options, no residual guarantees — clean. Lease liabilities R1,826k are immaterial to LTV (<0.03% of R6.0bn portfolio). Discount rate = Prime.

- Valuation reconciliation: R563,296k + R13,504k SL accrual = **R576,800k** ✓ ties to property list total.
- Property list sum: 17,000 + 88,000 + 135,000 + 150,000 + 38,800 + 65,000 + 18,000 + 65,000 = **R576,800k** ✓.
- GLA sum: 2,080 + 15,991 + 7,254 + 14,148 + 0 + 6,084 + 2,012 + 6,869 = **54,438m²** ✓.
- Disposal list sum: 23,500 + 42,000 + 68,000 + 75,000 + 580,000 = **R788,500k** ✓.

- Share capital Group: 5,375,385 + 95,620 = **5,471,005k** ✓.
- Share count: 1,840,323,952 + 250,000,000 = **2,090,323,952** ✓; less treasury 44,829,030 = **2,045,494,922** ✓.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `*` — Note 15, p. 248 (non-cash borrowings repaid R689,866k)**
- **Quote**: "Representing amounts paid by transferring attorneys directly to lenders for disposals as well as the settlement of notes by way of offsetting old facilities with new facilities at funders. (custody settlements - during the year ended 31 March 2025)."
- **Implication**: The R689,866k non-cash repayment is a **mixed** figure — part disposal-linked (attorneys paying lenders directly from sale proceeds) and part custody settlement (old facilities offset against new facilities at funders, i.e., refinancing rollovers). This means the R689,866k is **not** all genuine debt reduction — some is refinancing that leaves economic debt unchanged. This is critical for forecasting: the true cash debt reduction from disposals is smaller than R689,866k. **Must verify**: split between disposal-linked and custody-settlement components; whether custody settlements are FY2025-only (footnote wording is ambiguous — "during the year ended 31 March 2025" may qualify only the custody settlements, or the whole footnote).

**Footnote `*` — Note 15, p. 249 (facilities settled from disposal proceeds)**
- **Quote**: "These facilities were settled during the year with disposals proceeds."
- **Implication**: RMB O (R185,144k), RMB J (R50,750k), RMB share loan (R125,665k), RMB M (R113,930k), RMB N (R16,742k) = **R492,231k** of facilities were settled from disposal proceeds. This is a hard number for the disposal-proceeds-to-debt application (Q197/Q32/Q129). **Must verify**: whether the R492,231k is included in the R689,866k non-cash repayment or is separate; Accelerate portion.

**Footnote `*` — Note 16, p. 250 (Rebuilt Claim derecognition)**
- **Quote**: "During the current financial year, management assessed that no present enforceable obligation exists in respect of the Rebuilt Claim, having regard to the lapsing of the 2022 and 2024 Settlement Agreements and all other relevant facts and circumstances. The provision has accordingly been derecognised."
- **Implication**: The R300,000k related-party payable (Rebuilt Claim provision) was **derecognised** — a R300,000k credit. This is a **non-cash, non-distributable** item that must be excluded from SA REIT FFO/distributable earnings. The wording "no present enforceable obligation exists" is a management assertion, not a legal determination — **must verify** against the contingent liabilities note (Q74) and legal proceedings note. The credit's P&L line is still not disclosed (Q7/Q27/Q45/Q72/Q155).

**Footnote `**` — Note 16, p. 250 (interest accrual on derivatives R2.4m)**
- **Quote**: "Includes an interest accrual relating to derivatives of R2,4 million for 31 March 2026."
- **Implication**: Derivatives are in a **net payable** position (R2.4m interest accrual). This is small but confirms the swap book is cash-settling against the REIT. **Must verify**: swap MTM, notional, % hedged (Q31/Q88/Q153).

**Footnote `*` — Note 17, p. 251 (Retail rent 2025 includes R61.8m Headlease rental income)**
- **Quote**: "Retail rent for 31 March 2025 includes R61,8 million Headlease rental income. Due to the lapse of the 2024 Settlement Agreement, all terms of previous Agreements were adhered to and accordingly actioned. That had the effect of raising additional Headlease rent for the period 1 April 2024 to 30 November 2024, that were previously cancelled in the Settlement Agreement."
- **Implication**: The FY2025 retail rental comparative (R378,187k) is **inflated by R61.8m** of one-off Headlease rent. Normalised FY2025 retail rent ≈ R316,387k. FY2026 retail rent R286,682k vs normalised R316,387k = −9.4% (not −24.2% as headline suggests). This is a **critical normalisation** for like-for-like NPI forecasting. **Must verify**: whether the R61.8m is cash or accrual; whether any FY2026 reversal/refund is expected; the Headlease counterparty (related party?).

**Footnote `*` — Note 18, p. 252 (Property management fees 2025 included R6.8m APMC)**
- **Quote**: "Property management fees for 31 March 2025 included R6,8 million due to APMC as a result of the lapsed Settlement Agreement."
- **Implication**: FY2025 property management fees (R13,803k) are inflated by R6.8m APMC fee. Normalised FY2025 ≈ R7,003k. FY2026 R10,225k vs normalised R7,003k = +46% — a real increase, not a decrease. **Must verify**: APMC related-party status and whether FY2026 includes any APMC fee.

**Footnote `#` — Note 18, p. 252 (Other property expenses 2025 included R5.1m APMC commission)**
- **Quote**: "Other property expenses for 31 March 2025 included R5,1 million relating to commission due to APMC as a result of the lapsed Settlement Agreement. Other property expenses includes items such as property related professional fees, advertising and promotional costs, parking service level agreements, airconditioning, meter reading and private refuse removal costs."
- **Implication**: FY2025 other property expenses (R46,212k) inflated by R5.1m APMC commission. Normalised ≈ R41,112k. FY2026 R33,261k vs normalised R41,112k = −19.1%. **Must verify**: APMC related-party status; whether FY2026 includes any APMC commission.

**Note 15 qualification — "Carrying value approximates the fair value of borrowings"**
- **Quote**: "Carrying value approximates the fair value of borrowings. Interest payments are made as they fall due and capital repayments are only made as per the maturity dates above or extended on the appropriate date. Interest rates on these loans are market related and at arm's length with third party lenders."
- **Implication**: No fair-value hierarchy disclosure for debt; no hedge accounting effectiveness statement. "Extended on the appropriate date" implies extension options exist but terms are not disclosed. **Must verify**: extension option terms, milestone definitions, consequences (Q71/Q86).

**Note 15 qualification — "Interest rates on these loans are market related and at arm's length"**
- **Implication**: No related-party debt disclosed — all lenders are third-party. This is a positive governance signal but does not address the DMTN noteholders.

In South Africa, capital gains taxation is not applicable on the sale of investment property and shares in a REIT or property
Company, in terms of Section 25BB of the Income Tax Act applicable to REITs. Consequently, no deferred tax was raised on
the fair value adjustments recognised in respect of investment property. Allowances relating to immovable property can no
longer be claimed by a REIT and if a REIT sells immovable property, any allowances claimed on properties prior to becoming
a REIT will be recouped. Despite a loss being reflected for the Group and a profit for the Company, no tax is payable by the
company following large bad debts written off.

- **Q18 / Q51 / Q150 / Q162 (Insurance R82,5m 50% share, FFO exclusion, cash flow line)**
  - **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D020 REIT Disclosures / D013)`
  - **Answer & evidence**: Note 19 confirms "Insurance claim received" of R82,500k in both Group and Company for FY2026 (nil in FY2025) [D018.7, p. 253]. This is the same R82,5m figure flagged earlier as a 50%-share insurance item. It is presented as **other income**, not netted against property expenses, and is therefore a non-recurring, non-property-operating item that must be excluded from SA REIT FFO/distributable earnings. The cash flow line and the 50%-share basis (i.e., why only half of a gross claim) are still not evidenced here — carry forward.

It is a one-off, non-recurring, non-distributable item and must be excluded from FFO/distributable earnings. This also links to Q73/Q44 (related-party receivable write-off) — the VAT component recovered is R84,247k.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 19 footnote `#` — VAT refund R84,247k** [D018.7, p. 253]: "The VAT refund relates to the recovery of the VAT component from SARS on the write-off of the related party receivable." This is critical: the R84,247k is **not operating other income** — it is a one-off cash recovery tied to the related-party receivable write-off (Q73/Q44). It must be **excluded from SA REIT FFO and distributable earnings**. It also means part of the previously written-off exposure has been recovered in cash — relevant to the contingent-asset question (Q28). Verify in D020 whether the REIT's distributable-earnings bridge strips this out.

- **Note 20 footnote `*` — Salaries FY2025 APMC recovery** [D018.7, p. 253]: "Salaries and other staff costs for 31 March 2025 includes a recovery due from APMC for salaries paid by the Company as a result of the lapsed Settlement Agreement." Confirms APMC is a related party and that FY2025 staff costs were distorted by a recovery. Normalised staff cost base ≈ R22,339k (FY2026) vs R21,403k (FY2025) — the FY2025 figure is not clean. Verify APMC related-party status and whether any FY2026 residual recovery exists (Q208/Q209/Q90).

- **Note 21 footnotes 1–6 — Board changes** [D018.7, p. 255]: Wandrag retired 31 Aug 2024; Pydigadu appointed 1 Sep 2025; Day appointed 1 Feb 2025; **Georgiou resigned 15 Oct 2025**; Mboweni passed away 12 Oct 2024; van der Merwe resigned 10 Jul 2025. Confirms the Georgiou 12-month JSE related-party window (Q90) runs to ~15 Oct 2026 — relevant for FY2027 related-party transaction disclosure. Also confirms prescribed officer = Pieter Grobler (Q94 resolved).

- **Note 22 — Fair Value Adjustments** [D018.7, p. 255]: The R428,888k investment-property FV loss is the "R428,9m narrative" figure — now fully reconciled. Key point: the **R8,558k "disposal adjustments"** is a separate FV line from the disposal gain, and the **R27,965k held-for-sale FV loss** is embedded in the total. All are non-cash and must be excluded from distributable earnings. The **R312,010k Company subsidiary FV loss** is a separate non-cash item (Q105). Verify in D020 that the distributable-earnings bridge excludes all three.

- **Note 23 footnotes `*` and `#`** [D018.7, p. 256]:
  - `*`: FY2025 "Interest – other" included **R71,1m accrued interest** from the July 2024 Settlement Agreement, **reversed in November 2024** when the agreement lapsed. This is a large non-cash FY2025 distortion — the FY2025 finance-cost base is not comparable. Normalised FY2026 finance costs ≈ R397,841k.
  - `#`: FY2025 RMB share loan interest of **R12,6m was misclassified** as "interest – other" and has been restated into the RMB SPV line. Confirms the FY2025 comparative is restated — use restated figures for forecasting.
  - **Debt structuring fees amortised R15,647k** (FY2025: R42,473k) — the FY2025 figure was inflated; FY2026 is the cleaner run-rate. This is the non-cash EIR component (Q210).

- **Note 24 — Finance Income** [D018.7, p. 256]: Confirms **no related-party interest in FY2026** (FY2025: R98,512k) — the written-off receivable no longer accrues. Group external interest is now only banks (R6,050k) + Eskom deposits (R1,063k) + tenants (R312k). Company intercompany interest R105,776k is eliminated on consolidation. This resolves the finance-income collapse (Q141) and the intra-group elimination (Q156).

- **Note 25 — Taxation** [D018.7, p. 257]: Key qualifications:
  - **No deferred tax on investment-property FV adjustments** (Section 25BB REIT exemption) — confirms FV losses are non-taxable, so no deferred-tax asset/liability to model.
  - **"Derecognition of related party payable (81,000)"** — a R81,000k non-cash tax-reconciliation adjustment, corroborating the Rebuilt Claim / related-party payable derecognition (Q140/Q205). Verify whether this is part of the R300,000k Rebuilt Claim or a separate R81,000k item.
  - **"No tax is payable by the company following large bad debts written off"** — confirms the tax loss position is driven by the related-party write-off; no cash tax to model near-term.
  - **Assessed loss (34,648) Group / (46,530) Company** — a tax asset being recognised; verify recoverability assumption.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

**Q157 / Q199 / Q89 / Q110 (weighted average shares, treasury, share capital)**
- **Status**: `Resolved`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 29 [D018.8, p. 262] discloses: shares in issue at beginning 1,795,868,398; rights issue 250,000,000; shares in issue at end 2,045,868,398; **weighted average number of shares in issue 1,970,950,395** (FY2025: 1,810,936,713). Footnote `*` explains the rights offer at 40c vs ruling price 43c triggered an IAS 33 bonus-factor adjustment to comparatives; prior-year weighted average was previously disclosed as 1,708,967,075. No dilutive instruments. This resolves the weighted-average share count needed for FFO/NAV per share. Note: the 2,045,868,398 shares in issue is gross of the 44,829,303 treasury shares flagged earlier (Q198) — treasury treatment in the weighted average is not explicitly stated and should be confirmed.

**Q198 (treasury share count 44,829,030 vs 44,829,303)**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D018.8/D020)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 29 [D018.8, p. 262] gives shares in issue 2,045,868,398 but does not reconcile to treasury shares. The 273-share discrepancy remains open; no treasury reconciliation in this section.

**Q89 (rights offer 250m @40c = R100,0m)**
- **Status**: `Resolved`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 29 [D018.8, p. 262] confirms 250,000,000 shares issued on implementation of the rights offer in July 2025 at 40 cents (footnote `*`), consistent with R100,0m gross. Bonus factor applied per IAS 33.

**Q73 / Q28 / Q44 / Q122 / Q154 (related-party write-off, ECL, residual receivable, contingent asset)**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open)`
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 28 [D018.8, pp. 260–261] itemises the FY2025 ECL provisions and FY2026 bad-debt write-offs by counterparty:
  - Fourways Precinct: ECL provision FY2025 (792,163); bad debt write-off FY2026 (792,163)
  - Azrapart: ECL provision FY2025 (32,868); write-off FY2026 (32,868)
  - Michael Family Trust: ECL provision FY2025 (144,290); write-off FY2026 (144,290)
  - APMC: ECL provision FY2025 (1,385); write-off FY2026 (1,385)
  - **Total FY2025 ECL provision = 970,706; total FY2026 write-off = 970,706** — this reconciles to the R970,7m narrative [D018.8, p. 261].
  - Note 26 [D018.8, p. 258] shows FY2026 ECL charge of only R10,029k Group (FY2025: R1,046,461k), confirming the large prior-year provision is not repeated.
  - **Residual receivable / contingent asset**: Note 28 shows all related-party balances now nil at 31 Mar 2026 (loans, guarantees, headlease receivable all "–"). The contingent asset question (recovery of written-off debt) is **not** addressed in this section — still open.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `*` — Note 29, weighted average shares [D018.8, p. 262]**
- **Text**: "The rights offer was concluded at 40 cents per share which was less than the ruling price on the day of 43 cents per share. Therefore a bonus factor was calculated (in terms of IAS 33) resulting in an adjustment in the comparative information previously issued. The weighted average number of shares in issue was 1 708 967 075 (previously disclosed in prior year financials) prior to the change in comparative resulting from the bonus factor calculation."
- **Implication**: The FY2025 weighted average of 1,810,936,713 is **restated** from the previously disclosed 1,708,967,075 due to the IAS 33 bonus factor. This means FY2025 per-share metrics (loss per share, headline loss per share, DIPS, NAV per share) in the prior-year comparatives are **not directly comparable** to previously published figures. For forecasting, use the restated 1,970,950,395 (FY2026) and 1,810,936,713 (FY2025 restated) as the denominators. **Verification**: confirm whether the FY2025 DIPS/DPS per share in D004/D020 have been restated for the bonus factor, or whether they are on the old 1,708,967,075 basis — a mismatch would distort YoY DIPS growth.

**Footnote `*` — Note 28, Wanooka loan [D018.8, p. 260]**
- **Text**: "A large settlement was made against the loan due by Wanooka Properties Proprietary Limited on 31 March 2026."
- **Implication**: Wanooka loan receivable fell from R559,525k to R7,557k; loan payable fell from R507,495k to nil. This is a **R551,968k receivable reduction** and **R507,495k payable reduction** — a net R44,473k cash/asset movement. The settlement on the last day of the financial year (31 March 2026) is a **post-balance-sheet-event-adjacent** item that materially affects the Company's loan balances and interest income run-rate (FY2026 interest income R55,515k vs FY2025 R46,534k — the FY2026 figure includes a full year on the pre-settlement balance). **Verification**: confirm the settlement mechanism (cash vs set-off vs capitalisation), whether it is a related-party transaction requiring JSE disclosure, and the FY2027 interest income run-rate on the residual R7,557k.

**Note 28 qualification — Georgiou related-party window [D018.8, p. 259]**
- **Text**: "No transactions occurred with any of these entities since 1 April 2025 to 15 October 2025 apart from non-executive director fees paid as disclosed in note 21."
- **Implication**: This is a **positive confirmation** that the FY2026 related-party transactions with Georgiou entities (the R970,706k write-off) relate to **pre-FY2026 balances**, not new FY2026 transactions. It supports the treatment of the write-off as a prior-year ECL provision being written off in FY2026 (non-cash, no FY2026 P&L impact beyond the R10,029k ECL charge). **Verification**: confirm the R970,706k write-off is entirely against FY2025-provisioned balances and has **no FY2026 P&L charge** — i.e., the FY2026 ECL charge of R10,029k is unrelated new provisioning.

**Note 28 qualification — "All transactions with related parties are at arm's length" [D018.8, p. 259]**
- **Implication**: Standard boilerplate, but given the R970,7m write-off and the Azrapart 50% co-ownership of Fourways Mall, the arm's-length assertion should be tested against the JSE related-party fair-opinion process. **Verification**: confirm whether the Azrapart payable derecognition (R300,000k) and the Fourways Precinct write-off (R792,163k) were subject to JSE related-party disclosure/fair-opinion.

**Note 26 — "Derecognition of related party payable (300,000)" [D018.8, p. 258]**
- **Implication**: This is presented as a **non-cash add-back** in the cash flow reconciliation, meaning it increased operating profit before working capital changes by R300,000k. But the corresponding **income statement credit** is not visible in this section. If the R300,000k was credited to P&L (other income), it would inflate FY2026 profit before tax — yet Note 26 shows a **loss before tax of R45,888k** Group, which is after the R423,412k FV loss and the R300,000k derecognition credit. **Verification**: confirm the P&L line for the R300,000k derecognition and whether it is excluded from SA REIT distributable earnings (it is non-cash and one-off, so should be excluded).

**Note 26 — "VAT refund on written off debt (84,247)" [D018.8, p. 258]**
- **Implication**: Presented as a **negative adjustment** (i.e., deducted) in the cash flow reconciliation, meaning it reduced operating profit before working capital changes. This is consistent with it being a **non-operating recovery** credited to other income [D018.7, p. 253] and then removed for cash flow purposes. **Verification**: confirm the cash flow line where the R84,247k cash receipt actually appears (investing? operating?) — if it is in operating cash flow, the reconciliation treatment is inconsistent.

**Note 26 — "Debt structuring fee amortisation 14,759" vs Note 23 R15,647k [D018.8, p. 258 vs D018.7, p. 256]**
- **Implication**: **R888k discrepancy** between the cash flow add-back (R14,759k) and the Note 23 finance cost amortisation (R15,647k). This is a new reconciliation anomaly. **Verification**: confirm which figure is correct and whether the difference is a Company/Group split or a classification difference.

**Note 26 — "Financing income (7,425)" Group vs "(113,113)" Company [D018.8, p. 258]**
- **Implication**: The Company financing income of R113,113k (FY2025: R196,892k) is much larger than Group R7,425k, reflecting intra-group interest that eliminates on consolidation. This is consistent with Note 24 [D018.7, p. 256]. **Verification**: confirm the R113,113k Company financing income composition (Wanooka R55,515k + Pybus R37,726k + Parktown R12,535k + Accelerate Treasury = R105,776k + external R7,337k ≈ R113,113k) — arithmetic ties approximately.

**Note 26 — "Dividend income (49,644)" Company only [D018.8, p. 258]**
- **Implication**: Company dividend income R49,644k (FY2025: R15,940k) from subsidiaries (Parktown R36,100k + Wanooka R13,544k = R49,644k per Note 28 [D018.8, p. 260]). This eliminates on consolidation. **Verification**: confirm no FY2026 dividend income from Azrapart or other related parties.

**Note 27 — Capital commitments [D018.8, p. 259]**
- **Implication**: Approved and committed R20,358k (to be spent within 2 months); approved but not committed R79,670k (3–18 months). Total R100,028k. This is **lower** than FY2025 total R195,552k, suggesting capex pipeline is winding down. **Verification**: confirm the nature of the R79,670k approved-but-not-committed (Fourways Mall remediation? solar? TI?) and whether it is included in the FY2027 capex forecast.

**Note 29 — Headline earnings reconciliation [D018.8, p. 262]**
- **Implication**: Loss attributable to owners (45,888) + change in FV of investment properties 428,888 = **headline earnings 383,000**. Note the FV adjustment used here is **R428,888k** (the investment-property-only figure from Note 22), not the R423,412k total FV adjustment in Note 26. The R5,476k difference is the derivative FV gain (Note 22). **Verification**: confirm the headline earnings adjustment excludes the derivative FV gain and the R300,000k derecognition — i.e., headline earnings of R383,000k still includes the R300,000k non-cash derecognition credit, which would **overstate** headline earnings. This is a critical FFO/distributable earnings adjustment point.

**Note 29 — Basic and diluted loss per share [D018.8, p. 262]**
- **Implication**: Basic loss per share (2.33c) = (45,888) / 1,970,950,395 × 100 = (2.33c) ✓. Headline EPS 19.43c = 383,000 / 1,970,950,395 × 100 = 19.43c ✓. Arithmetic ties. **Verification**: confirm the headline EPS of 19.43c is **not** the DIPS — DIPS should exclude the R300,000k derecognition and other non-distributable items.

  31. Financial Risk Management                                           
  The Board has overall responsibility for the establishment and oversight of the risk management framework. The Audit and
  Risk Committee reviews management’s compliance with the Group’s risk policies and procedures and assesses the adequacy
                                                                          
  of the risk management framework. The committee reports regularly to the Board.
                                                                          
  The Group’s risk management policies are established to identify and analyse the risks faced by the Group, to set appropriate
  risk limits and controls, and to monitor risks and adherence to limits. Risk management policies and systems are reviewed
  regularly to reflect changes in market conditions and the Group’s activities.
                                                                          
  The Audit and Risk Committee oversees how management monitors compliance with the risk management policies and
                                                                          
  procedures and reviews the adequacy of the risk management framework in relation to the risks faced by the Group. The Audit
  and Risk Committee is assisted in its oversight role by internal audit. Internal audit undertakes regular and ad hoc reviews of
  risk management controls and procedures, the results of which are reported to the Audit and Risk Committee.
                                                                          
  The Group has exposure to liquidity, market and credit risk from its use of financial instruments, which consist primarily of
  deposits with banks, interest-bearing liabilities, derivatives, trade and other receivables and trade and other payables.
                                                                          
                                                                          
                                                                          
  Liquidity Risk                                                          
  Liquidity risk is the risk that the Group will encounter difficulty in meeting the obligations associated with its financial liabilities
  that are settled by delivering cash or another financial asset. The Group mitigates its liquidity risk by effectively managing
  its working capital, capital expenditure and cash flows. The financing resources comprise a mixture of cash generated
                                                                          
  from operations and long- and short-term borrowings. Committed borrowing facilities are available for meeting liquidity
  requirements and the Company manages the liquidity risk through an ongoing review of commitments and credit facilities.
                                                                          
  Facilities are extended when they become due for maturity and when assets are disposed of, the facilities are repaid. Cash
  flow forecasts and budgets are prepared and adequate utilised borrowing facilities, disclosed in note 15, are monitored.
  Refer to note 35 for further disclosures and considerations.            
                                                                          
                                                                          
  The maturity profile of the contractual cash flows of financial liabilities, and financial assets held to mitigate the risk, are
  presented in the following table. The cash flows are undiscounted contractual amounts.
