 Market risk                                                              
 Market risk is the risk that changes in market prices, such as foreign exchange rates, interest rates and equity prices will
 affect the Group’s income or the value of its financial instruments. The objective of market risk management is to manage
 and control market risk exposures within acceptable parameters, while optimising the return.
                                                                          
                                                                          
                                                                          
 Interest rate risk                                                       
 The Group is exposed to interest rate risk through its variable rate cash balances, receivables and interest-bearing
 borrowings. The Group reduces its exposure to changes in interest rates by fixing interest rates in respect of its local
 borrowings. This is achieved by entering into swap agreements to receive variable and pay fixed interest rates. At year-
                                                                          
 end, interest rates for the Group were hedged at a level of 83,3% (2025: 53,6%) of total borrowings. Refer to note 9 for
 disclosure regarding interest rate swaps.                                
                                                                          
                                                                          
 Transition progress                                                      
 The Group will transition from JIBAR-linked instruments to ZARONIA-linked instruments. Any new contracts are now
                                                                          
 referenced to ZARONIA. Legacy contracts are being actively transitioned in line with market conventions and counterparties’
 readiness.                                                               
                                                                          
 As at the reporting date, the following instruments remain unmodified and continue to reference JIBAR:
                                                                          
 • Non-derivative financial liabilities: R3,0 billion                     
                                                                          
 • Derivative financial instruments: R2,5 billion                         
                                                                          
                                                                          
 These balances are expected to transition progressively as contracts mature or are renegotiated, but in any event will be
 transitioned before 31 December 2026.                                    
                                                                          
 The Group does not expect the IBOR reform to have a material impact on its financial position or performance and
 continues to monitor developments to ensure an orderly transition.       
                                                                          
 The all-in weighted average cost of interest-bearing borrowings for the Group (including derivatives) is 9,87% (2025: 10,89%).

Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk of financial loss to the Group if a customer or counterparty to a financial instrument fails to meet its
contractual obligations, and arises principally from trade receivables, cash and cash equivalents, loans to group companies
and derivatives. There is no significant concentration of credit risk as exposure is spread over a large number of counterparties.
The long-term issuer rating for First National Bank is zaAA.
The Company’s maximum exposure to credit risk by class of financial asset is as follows:

Credit risk management
Related party receivables and Headlease due from related party
The following factors are considered when assessing the recoverability of related party balances due:
• Historical receipts and reduction of the related party balances outstanding;
• The nature and timing of current and potential future related party transactions;
• The financial ability of the related parties to settle their obligations on the future considering their cash flow, net asset
value and security provided;
• The actual or expected operating results of the borrower; and
• Significant changes in external market factors.
In July 2024, the Company and Mr Georgiou (on behalf of the Related Parties signed a Settlement Agreement which would
have resulted in the settlement of amounts due from various entities to the Company. The Settlement Agreement would
have resulted in a net settlement of amounts due and payable with no outflow of cash for the Company. The Settlement
Agreement however lapsed during November 2024 as certain suspensive conditions were not met. Management redrafted
a New Settlement Agreement on substantially the same basis as the previous Settlement Agreement. The New Settlement
Agreement was however not concluded and due to legal actions instituted against the various Related Parties by third
parties, the amounts due from the Related Parties were fully impaired on 31 March 2025.

 31. Financial Risk Management (cont.)                                    
                                                                          
 In the current financial year, the outstanding amounts due from the Related Parties were written off. Despite the write off,
 the Company will continue to seek recovery of amounts due from the Related Parties. The Company does not accept the
 validity of the Rebuilt Claim asserted by Azrapart and maintains that no present enforceable obligation exists in respect
 thereof.                                                                 
                                                                          
                                                                          
                                                                          
 Loans and other receivables                                              
 The credit risk attached to loans due from group companies, loans due from related parties, and other receivables were
 assessed in terms of the general approach per IFRS 9.                    
                                                                          
 The Group assesses on a forward-looking basis the ECLs associated with loans and other receivables carried at amortised
                                                                          
 cost. This entails the assessment of credit risk since initial recognition, probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD)
 and exposure at default (EAD) [i.e. PD x LGD x EAD = ECL].               
                                                                          
 Forward-looking information on macro-economic factors affecting the ability of the clients to settle the receivable include:
                                                                          
 • Changes in economic, regulatory, technological and environmental factors (such as industry outlook, GDP, employment
   and politics); and                                                     
 • External market indicators.                                            
                                                                          
 • The Middle East Conflict impacts the following:                        
   – Energy and fuel prices increase following the crude oil price increases. This in turn could lead to logistics and supply
                                                                          
     chain disruptions and increases in food and fertiliser prices        
   – Inflation re-acceleration due to the increased fuel prices           
                                                                          
   – Interest rate path disruption as Government pauses the decrease of interest rates and increases transport and fuel
     prices                                                               
                                                                          
   – Currency weakness affecting import costs and impacting food and transport prices
                                                                          
 The credit risk is measured by assessing the status of performance during the financial year i.e. performing (stage 1) – loans
 whose credit risk is in line with original expectations; underperforming (stage 2) – loans for which a significant increase in
 credit risk has occurred compared to original expectations i.e. a significant increase in credit risk is presumed if the entity
 is displaying obvious signs of distress (Companies in technical insolvency and current liabilities exceeding current assets,
                                                                          
 requiring holding company support); and non-performing (stage 3) – interest and/or principal repayments are past due or
 it becomes probable a customer will enter business rescue or bankruptcy. The entity therefore displays obvious signs of
 distress. This assessment summarises the credit risk and how the ECL provision is determined for each of those categories.
                                                                          
 Loans and other receivables are segmented into counterparty type (i.e. income-generating property entity, property
 management, corporate, contractual property income) which assists with risk assessment. The probability of a loan defaulting
                                                                          
 has been determined using historical data up to 36 months from inception together with other pertinent information that is
 available. A summary of the assumptions underpinning the Group’s ECL model is as follows:

  hold income-generating assets with low vacancies. Accelerate Treasury holds shares in Accelerate Property Fund Limited (as

  at year-end. This resulted in the loan, initially advanced as stage 1, being moved to stage 3. The loans of both Pybus and

Trade receivables                                                         
Credit risk arises from the risk that a tenant may default or not meet its obligations timeously. Management has established
                                                                          
a credit policy under which each new tenant is analysed individually for creditworthiness before the Group’s standard
payment terms and conditions are offered, which include in certain cases the provision of a deposit. The financial position
of the tenants is monitored on an ongoing basis. Allowance is made for expected credit losses and credit risk is limited to
the carrying amount of the financial assets at financial year-end. There have been no significant changes in the credit risk
                                                                          
management policies and processes since the prior reporting period.       
                                                                          
The Group applies the IFRS 9 simplified approach to measuring expected credit losses which uses a lifetime expected loss
allowance for all trade receivables. To measure the expected credit losses, trade receivables have been grouped based on
shared credit risk characteristics and the days past due.                 
                                                                          
The expected loss rates are based on the payment profiles over a period of 36 months before 31 March 2026 and the
corresponding historical credit losses experienced within this period. To measure expected credit losses on an individual
                                                                          
basis, trade receivables are assessed net of the deposit or guarantee held. Arrears aged 90 days and over are in most
instances deemed to be irrecoverable and provided for. The expected loss rates are based on the Group’s historical credit
losses experienced over the period prior to the period end and are reassessed at each reporting date.
                                                                          
The Group uses a general approach to measure all other receivables per note 10. Under this approach each receivable is
assessed individually.                                                    
                                                                          
                                                                          
On that basis, the loss allowance as at 31 March 2026 was determined as follows for trade receivables, other receivables
and loans receivable.                                                     
                                                                          
The table below emphasises the overall ageing and not necessarily the split between National and small to medium
enterprises. National tenants have low level of arrears compared to small to medium enterprises.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

**Q14 / Q111 / Q154 (High): Fourways Mall bad-debt/arrears provision, tenant arrear aging, collection rate trend.**
- **Status**: `Resolved` (aging now disclosed)
- **Answer & evidence**: Group trade receivable aging at 31 Mar 2026 [D018.9, p. 276]: Current R13,136k; 30 days R3,612k; 60 days R2,091k; Over 90 days R33,487k; Total R52,326k. ECL allowance R14,932k (28.54% overall). Over-90-day gross R33,487k with ECL R12,217k (36.48%). Prior year (2025) over-90-day gross was R146,656k with ECL R90,241k (61.53%) — a dramatic improvement in aging. National retailers over-90-day R14,614k (ECL 43.0%); SMEs over-90-day R18,873k (ECL 31.5%). Note `**` [p. 276] flags that some high-value national tenants in 90+ days are excluded from ECL because payment arrangements are in place — this is a qualification to monitor.

**Q28 / Q44 / Q73 / Q122 (High): Related-party receivable residual, contingent asset, ECL.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved` (residual/contingent asset still open)
- **Answer & evidence**: Related party receivables R970,706k gross fully impaired (ECL R970,706k) at 31 Mar 2025; **nil** at 31 Mar 2026 [D018.9, p. 269]. Narrative [p. 269–270] confirms: Settlement Agreement lapsed Nov 2024; New Settlement Agreement not concluded; amounts fully impaired 31 Mar 2025; **written off in current year**; Company "will continue to seek recovery" and "does not accept the validity of the Rebuilt Claim asserted by Azrapart and maintains that no present enforceable obligation exists." This confirms the R300,000k Azrapart payable derecognition logic (Q205/Q230). Contingent asset recovery remains unquantified — still open.

**Q205 / Q230 / Q239 (High): R300,000k Azrapart payable derecognition — P&L line, FFO exclusion, residual liability.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved` (P&L line/FFO exclusion still open)
- **Answer & evidence**: Footnote `@` [D018.9, pp. 265, 267] confirms the 2025 comparatives were **restated** because "R300,0 million was incorrectly disclosed within this risk management note when the balance was not a financial instrument as per IFRS 9." This confirms the R300,000k was never a financial instrument (IFRS 9) — consistent with derecognition. Explicit SA REIT BPR distributable-earnings exclusion still to be confirmed in D020.

**Q206 (High): Derivatives — swap MTM, notional, % hedged, over-hedge risk.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved` (notional/hedge effectiveness still open)
- **Answer & evidence**: Hedged at **83.3%** of total borrowings (2025: 53.6%) [D018.9, p. 267]. Derivative financial instruments: asset R8,764k (one-to-five years), liability R3,190k [p. 265]. Net derivative FV R5,574k [p. 268]. Sensitivity: 0.25% swap FV move = R14k [p. 268]. Narrative [p. 268]: "total of R2.5 billion hedges in place. Therefore, the value exposed to fluctuations in interest rates is R500.0 million. The total exposure is thus limited to R5.0 million." This implies notional hedged ≈ R2.5bn against R3,002,017k debt = 83.3% — consistent. Over-hedge risk post Mar 2027 still open (all debt matures 31 Mar 27).

**Q210 / Q118 / Q236 / Q243 (High): Finance costs bridge — fee amortisation R14,759k vs R15,647k discrepancy.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved` (R888k discrepancy still open)
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 30 [D018.9, p. 263] confirms **debt fees amortised R14,759k** in the reconciliation of liabilities from financing activities — matching Note 26, not Note 23's R15,647k. The R888k discrepancy persists and is now triangulated across three notes (23, 26, 30). Still open for reconciliation.

**Q203 / Q204 (High): R689,866k non-cash repayment — split; reconcile to R788,500k gross disposal consideration.**
- **Status**: `Partially resolved` (split still open)
- **Answer & evidence**: Note 30 [D018.9, p. 263] shows non-cash "Repayment (689,866)" in interest-bearing borrowings, and separately Company "Repayment (512,093) (1,201,959)" in loans from group companies. Footnote `*` [p. 263] states: "Relates to cash proceeds on disposals and paid directly to facilities via the transferring attorneys." This confirms the R689,866k is disposal-linked (not custody settlements as previously hypothesised). The R1,201,959k Company figure appears to be a combined loans-from-group repayment. Split between disposal-linked and other still needs confirmation.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `#` [D018.9, p. 263] — "In the prior year R10,272 was restated as it was incorrectly included as a non-cash item."**
- This restates the FY2025 "Proceeds#" line in the Company column (loans from group companies) from a non-cash to a cash item. It confirms a prior-year classification error in the financing activities reconciliation. Implication: FY2025 comparative cash flow from financing is overstated/understated by R10,272k in the Company column. Must verify in D015 (cash flow statement) whether the restatement flows through to the face of the cash flow statement or only the note.

**Footnote `*` [D018.9, p. 263] — "Relates to cash proceeds on disposals and paid directly to facilities via the transferring attorneys."**
- This is the critical qualification: the R689,866k non-cash "Repayment" in interest-bearing borrowings is **disposal-linked** — cash proceeds from disposals paid directly to lenders by transferring attorneys, bypassing the Group's bank account. This means:
  - It is **not** a non-cash item in economic substance (cash did flow, just not through the Group's cash book).
  - It reconciles to the R788,500k gross disposal consideration (Q127) less amounts retained/settled to Accelerate (Q129) and other costs.
  - For the distributable-earnings bridge, this is a **balance sheet** movement, not a P&L item — no distributable-earnings impact, but it explains why disposal proceeds in the cash flow statement (R90,090k) are far below gross disposal consideration.
  - **Verification needed**: reconcile R689,866k to R788,500k gross disposal consideration; identify the R98,634k difference (retentions, costs, Accelerate portion).

**Footnote `@` [D018.9, pp. 265, 267] — "The 2025 Group/Company comparatives have been restated, R300,0 million was incorrectly disclosed within this risk management note when the balance was not a financial instrument as per IFRS 9."**
- This is a **material restatement qualification**. It confirms:
  - The R300,000k Azrapart "Rebuilt Claim" was **never a financial instrument** under IFRS 9 — it was a contingent/legal claim, not a contractual payable.
  - The FY2025 trade and other payables in the liquidity risk table are restated downward by R300,000k (Group: R83,856k restated vs original ~R383,856k; Company: R82,069k restated).
  - This reinforces Q205/Q230/Q239: the R300,000k derecognition in FY2026 is a **correction of a prior misclassification**, not a new economic event. For SA REIT BPR distributable earnings, this must be excluded as a non-cash, non-recurring accounting correction.
  - **Verification needed**: confirm the R300,000k restatement is reflected in D012 (Statement of Financial Position) comparative and D015 (cash flow) — and that the FY2026 "derecognition" credit in headline earnings (Q239) is explicitly excluded from distributable earnings.

**Footnote `*` [D018.9, p. 265] — "Excludes prepayments" (trade and other receivables).**
- The R120,765k Group / R123,870k Company trade and other receivables in the liquidity table exclude prepayments. This means the Statement of Financial Position trade and other receivables (R122,294k Group per D012) includes prepayments of ~R1,529k. Minor, but confirms the liquidity table is not directly comparable to the balance sheet line.

**Footnote `#` [D018.9, p. 265] — "Excludes income received in advance and VAT" (trade and other payables).**
- The R86,507k Group / R84,797k Company trade and other payables in the liquidity table exclude income received in advance (R10,509k per D018.6) and VAT. This reconciles: balance sheet trade and other payables ~R97,016k less R10,509k = R86,507k. Confirms the liquidity table is a financial-instrument-only view.

**Footnote `**` [D018.9, p. 276] — "National retailers include some high value tenants in 90 days plus that were considered separately for ECL purposes... These tenants are not provided for as the amounts due are considered recoverable."**
- This is a **critical ECL qualification**. It means the R14,932k ECL allowance **understates** the true expected loss because certain high-value national tenants in 90+ days are excluded from provisioning on the basis of payment arrangements or non-standard terms. The over-90-day gross of R33,487k includes these excluded amounts. **Verification needed**: quantify the excluded high-value national tenant exposure and assess recoverability — this is a potential hidden bad-debt risk for FY2027.

**Footnote `#` [D018.9, pp. 276–277] — "The split for gross trade debtors and expected credit loss between national retailers and small to medium enterprises was not done in the 2025 financial year."**
- Confirms the FY2025 comparative split (National R682k carrying / R3,007k ECL; SME R163,564k / R90,262k) [p. 278] is a **reconstruction**, not originally disclosed. The FY2025 total ECL of R93,269k reconciles to the FY2025 aging table ECL of R93,268k (R1k rounding). This is a disclosure enhancement, not a restatement of amounts.

**Footnote `#` [D018.9, p. 273] — "Prior year disclosure has been enhanced."**
- Confirms the FY2025 loans-from-group ECL movement table is a disclosure enhancement, not a restatement. The FY2025 closing balances (Accelerate Treasury stage 3 R308,632k; Pybus stage 1 R390,390k; Wanooka stage 1 R559,525k) reconcile to the FY2026 opening balances [p. 272].

**Narrative qualification [D018.9, p. 270] — "The Company does not accept the validity of the Rebuilt Claim asserted by Azrapart and maintains that no present enforceable obligation exists in respect thereof."**
- This is a **legal position qualification**. It confirms management's view that the R300,000k Azrapart claim is not a valid liability. Combined with the IFRS 9 restatement footnote `@`, this supports the derecognition. However, it also flags **contingent liability risk**: if Azrapart's legal action succeeds, the R300,000k could crystallise. **Verification needed**: confirm legal status of Azrapart's claim and any provision/contingent liability disclosure in D018 (Note 28 or contingent liabilities note).

**Narrative qualification [D018.9, p. 271] — "Pybus holds the Citi Bank asset. The value of this asset changed materially due to the change in the bulk rate applied to the valuation. This change resulted in the entity requiring support from Accelerate... The credit risk associated with Pybus increased... This resulted in the loan, initially advanced as stage 1, being moved to stage 3."**
- This is a **material credit risk qualification**. Pybus Sixty-Two (RF) loan of R419,855k moved from stage 1 to stage 3 due to a **bulk rate change** on the Citi Bank asset valuation. ECL on Pybus is only R1,619k (0.39% LGD) — but the stage 3 classification signals significant credit deterioration. **Verification needed**: quantify the Citi Bank asset valuation change, the bulk rate assumption, and whether the R1,619k ECL is adequate given stage 3 status.

**Narrative qualification [D018.9, p. 271] — "Accelerate Treasury holds shares in Accelerate Property Fund Limited (as treasury shares) and remains in stage 3... The treasury loan has been specifically impaired to the entity's underlying net asset value which is linked to the shares held in Accelerate."**
- This confirms the Accelerate Treasury loan (R308,667k) is impaired to the **NAV of the treasury shares** — i.e., the ECL of R278,183k reflects the market value of Accelerate shares held. This is a **look-through NAV impairment**, not a credit event. **Verification needed**: confirm the treasury share count and NAV per share used in the impairment calculation; assess whether further impairment is likely if the share price/NAV declines.

**Narrative qualification [D018.9, p. 267] — "The Group will transition from JIBAR-linked instruments to ZARONIA-linked instruments... As at the reporting date, the following instruments remain unmodified and continue to reference JIBAR: Non-derivative financial liabilities: R3,0 billion; Derivative financial instruments: R2,5 billion... will be transitioned before 31 December 2026."**
- This is a **forward-looking qualification** with forecast implications: the entire debt book (R3.0bn) and hedge book (R2.5bn) will transition to ZARONIA before 31 Dec 2026. ZARONIA is typically lower than JIBAR (compounded ZARONIA vs 3m JIBAR spread), which could reduce interest costs — but the transition may also involve basis risk and hedge ineffectiveness. **Verification needed**: quantify the expected ZARONIA vs JIBAR spread impact on finance costs; confirm hedge accounting treatment post-transition.

**Narrative qualification [D018.9, p. 268] — "Although the above sensitivity reflects an increase/(decrease) of R30.0 million if interest rates move by 1%, the Group has a total of R2.5 billion hedges in place. Therefore, the value exposed to fluctuations in interest rates is R500.0 million. The total exposure is thus limited to R5.0 million."**
- This is a **hedging effectiveness qualification**. It confirms:
  - Gross debt R3,002,017k; hedged R2,500,000k (83.3%); unhedged R502,017k.
  - 1% rate move on unhedged debt = R5.0m impact (not R30.0m).
  - The R30.0m sensitivity in the table is the **gross** sensitivity before hedging; the **net** sensitivity is R5.0m.
  - **Verification needed**: confirm the R2.5bn hedge notional and the R500m unhedged exposure; assess over-hedge risk if debt is repaid from disposals before hedge maturity (all debt matures 31 Mar 27, hedges one-to-five years per p. 265 — potential over-hedge).

**Narrative qualification [D018.9, p. 268] — "The long-term issuer rating for First National Bank is zaAA."**
- Confirms FNB is the primary banking counterparty. Minor, but relevant for counterparty credit risk on cash (R110,456k) and derivatives (R8,764k).

**Narrative qualification [D018.9, p. 264] — "Refer to note 35 for further disclosures and considerations."**
- This is a **cross-reference lead**. Note 35 is not in this section capture — it likely contains the ICR covenant schedule, going concern, and/or capital management disclosures. **Verification needed**: capture Note 35 (likely in D018.10 or D019) to resolve Q212/Q23/Q52/Q70/Q87 (ICR covenants) and Q211 (refinancing).

33. Financial Covenants
The Group’s objective when managing capital (which includes share capital, borrowings, working capital and cash and cash
equivalents) is to maintain a flexible capital structure that reduces the cost of capital to an acceptable level of risk and to
safeguard the Group’s ability to continue as a going concern while taking advantage of strategic opportunities to maximise
stakeholder returns sustainably. To effectively manage the capital structure, the Group may adjust the amount of dividends
paid to shareholders, issue new shares or sell assets to reduce debt.

  34. Fair Value Hierarchy                                                 
  IFRS 13 requires that an entity disclose, for each class of financial instrument and investment property measured at fair value,
  the level in the fair value hierarchy into which the fair value measurements are categorised in their entirety.
                                                                           
  The fair value hierarchy reflects the significance of the inputs used in making fair value measurements.
                                                                           
  The level in the fair value hierarchy within which the fair value measurement is categorised in its entirety shall be determined
                                                                           
  on the basis of the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement in its entirety.

--- Section D018.10 | original physical page 283 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 32,33,34,35,36 ---
The fair value hierarchy has the following levels:
Level 1 - quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.
Level 2 - i nputs other than quoted prices included within level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability, either directly
(i.e. as prices) or indirectly (i.e. derived from prices).
Level 3 - inputs for the asset or liability that are not based on observable market data (unobservable inputs).

 35. Going Concern                                                       
 The preparation of financial statements in accordance with IFRS Accounting Standards requires, based on the Conceptual
 Framework of IFRS Accounting Standards, that the financial statements be prepared on the underlying assumption that the
 entity (“entity” being the Company and the Group) is a going concern. This assumption presumes that an entity will continue
                                                                         
 in operation in the foreseeable future or, if that presumption is not valid, disclosure and a different basis of reporting are
 required. The Board of directors (“Board”) believes that as of the date of this report, this presumption is still appropriate and
 accordingly the financial statements have been prepared on the going concern basis. The Board has based this assumption
 on the considerations more fully explained throughout this note.        
                                                                         
 • The Group and Company reported a net loss of R45,8 million and a profit of R36,0 million for the 2026 reporting period,
   respectively. This loss is mainly attributable to the revaluation of investment property to its fair values and high finance
   costs. The position improved from the prior year’s net loss of R1,3 billion and R1,2 billion for the Group and the Company
                                                                         
   respectively. The prior year’s net loss was mainly as a result of the related party impairments.
 • The Group and company’s total assets of R6,8 billion and R7,6 billion exceed the total liabilities by R3,7 billion and
   R3,8 billion at 31 March 2026, respectively.                          
                                                                         
 • The Group had a covenant LTV of 43,3% in comparison to 47,6% in the prior year. This current year’s ratio does not exceed
   the covenant set by the lenders of 50,0%. The Group’s interest cover ratio of 1,2 times is equal to that of the prior year of
   1,2 times and above the covenant set by the funders at 1,1 times for year-end.
                                                                         
 • The Group’s current liabilities exceed its current assets (including non-current assets held-for-sale) by R2,3 billion.
   The company’s current liabilities of R3,8 billion exceed its current assets by R3,0 billion. The excess of current liabilities
   over current assets is as a result of the Group’s funding facilities maturing at 31 March 2027 and reflected as short-term.
                                                                         
   The facilities were reduced substantially with the disposal of assets and the raising of capital through a fully funded rights
   offer.                                                                
 • In further improving the Group financial position, the Board is committed to reduce its debt exposure to an overall debt
                                                                         
   level of R1,4 billion, LTV of below 40% and an ICR of 1,6 times following the implementation of the strategy. The strategy
   includes the following aspects:                                       
   – Disposing of assets that will achieve and improve the overall fundamental metrics relating to LTV and ICR as indicated
                                                                         
     above.                                                              
   – The finalisation of the appointment of Flanagan and Gerard and the Moolman Group, well known and respected
     retail experts, to asset and property manage Fourways Mall to further improve the overall fundamentals of the mall
                                                                         
     including to improve cash flow and reduce vacancies.                
   – A strategic plan to support the above initiatives and increased disposal plan.
                                                                         
                                                                         
 Solvency                                                                
 At 31 March 2026, independent valuations and desktop valuations of the investment property portfolio indicate that their
                                                                         
 fair values exceed the external debt of the Group. The covenant LTV ratio of 43,3% indicates a stable level however, the Group
 identified assets for disposal to improve the ICR as well as the LTV levels. The quantum of required disposals is considered
 achievable in the current market conditions.                            

--- Section D018.10 | original physical page 288 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 32,33,34,35,36 ---
                                                                         
  35. Going Concern (cont.)                                              
  Liquidity                                                              
                                                                         
  In assessing the Group’s liquidity, management prepared a cash flow forecast up until 31 March 2028, taking into consideration
  its restructure plan and other initiatives which indicate that the Group will have sufficient cash resources for the foreseeable
  future which is defined as 12 months from the date of publishing these financial statements. Operational cash flows are
  strong and evident from the cash flow statement.                       
                                                                         
  Cash flows and liquidity are monitored daily by management with oversight from the Board. Management has considered a
  number of estimates, judgements and assumptions in performing the liquidity assessments, the most significant of which
  are listed and expanded upon below:                                    
                                                                         
  • Facilities and corporate paper (notes) will mature on 31 March 2027 with discussion currently underway with funders to
    extend beyond the maturity date.                                     
                                                                         
  • The reduction in debt through the sale of properties. These have been earmarked as indicated in note 12.
  • The further reduction of vacancies in Fourways Mall and the increase in rental rates through the implementation of the
                                                                         
    Asset and Property management function to below existing levels.     
  • Fourways Mall capital expenditure (patially funded by working capital and facilities) and tenant installation allowances
    have been considered and modelled.                                   
                                                                         
                                                                         
  Conclusion                                                             
  The Board is of the view that given the significant headroom in the fair value of the assets over the fair value of the liabilities
                                                                         
  of R3,7 billion for the Group and R3,8 billion for the Company, the Group and Company remain solvent as at 31 March 2026
  and at the date of this report.                                        
                                                                         
  The ability of the Group to repay debt as it becomes due is dependent on the timing and quantum of cash flows from
  operations according to forecasts prepared by management, including scenario analyses, the ability to realise cash through
  the sale of properties identified as held-for-sale to the business and the ability to extend loan facilities beyond scheduled
                                                                         
  maturity dates.                                                        
                                                                         
  The Board has no intention to cease trading, curtail operations or liquidate properties in excess of those already earmarked
  for sale, other than the orderly disposals that may be necessary to reduce debt. The Board remains focused on and committed
  to the operations of the Group and Company and the repayment of debt.  
                                                                         
  The Board acknowledges the uncertainty related to the sale of disposal assets.
                                                                         
  Notwithstanding the acknowledgement of these uncertain events and having considered the validity of the principal
                                                                         
  assumptions set out above, including continued support from the Group’s principal financiers, the Board has concluded that
  the Company and Group are able to discharge liabilities in the normal course of business and is of the opinion that the going
  concern assumption is appropriate in the preparation of the financial statements.

--- Section D018.10 | original physical page 289 | area selection | Mixed / unspecified | Notes 32,33,34,35,36 ---
                                                                           
                                                                           
  36. Events after the Reporting Period                                    
                                                                           
  Subsequent to year end, the following properties were transferred as part of the Group’s strategy to improve the financial
  metrics of the fund. The net disposal proceeds amount to:                
                                                                           
  • The Buzz Shopping Centre – R150,0 million                              
  • Waterford – R65,0 million                                              
                                                                           
  • The Buzz vacant land – R38,8 million                                   
  • Valleyview – R16,2 million                                             
  • Edgars Polokwane – R24,1 million                                       
                                                                           
                                                                           
  Following these disposals the vacancies reduced from 10,9% to 8,4% and the LTV reduced from 43,3% to 41,1%.
                                                                           
  A sale agreement was concluded for the disposal of BMW Fourways at a selling price of R174,0 million. Upon transfer of the
  asset, the LTV will decrease further to 39,6%.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `*` — Note 32, p. 279 [D018.10]:**
> "* Excludes pre-payments"

Changes the headline: Group trade and other receivables financial-instrument figure R120,765k excludes prepayments. D012 trade and other receivables R122,294k − R120,765k = **R1,529k prepayments**. Company R123,870k. This is a classification note only — no distributable-earnings impact. Must verify prepayments R1,529k tie to D012 breakdown.

**Footnote `#` — Note 32, p. 279 [D018.10]:**
> "# Excludes income received in advance and VAT payable."

Changes the headline: Group trade and other payables financial-instrument figure R86,507k excludes income received in advance (D018.6: R10,509k) and VAT payable. Company R84,797k. **Critical reconciliation gap**: R86,507k is materially larger than D018.6 trade payables R17,929k — the R86,507k must include other payables/accruals not separately disclosed. Must reconcile to D012/D018.6 total trade and other payables.

**Footnote `*` — Note 32, p. 280 [D018.10] (FY2025 comparative restatement):**
> "* The 2025 group and company comparatives have been restated, R300,0 million was incorrectly disclosed within this risk management note when the balance was not a financial instrument as per IFRS 9."

**This is the most consequential footnote in the section.** It confirms the R300,000k Azrapart Rebuilt Claim was **incorrectly classified as a financial instrument** in the FY2025 risk-management note. FY2025 Group trade and other payables restated from R432,274k (implied) to **R132,274k**; Company from R429,136k (implied) to **R129,136k**. This corroborates Q205/Q230/Q239 — the R300,000k is **not** an IFRS 9 financial instrument. **Distributable-earnings implication**: the FY2026 derecognition credit of R300,000k (Note 26/28) is a non-cash, non-operating item that must be excluded from SA REIT distributable earnings and FFO. Explicit BPR exclusion still not stated in this section — carried forward as Q267.

**Note 33 qualification — RMB SPV LTV breach [D018.10, pp. 281–282]:**
> "At 31 March 2025, the LTV of the RMB security SPV was in breach at year-end and communicated to the funder. The breach was condoned by RMB subsequent to year end and was remedied with the disposal of Portside which transferred in January 2026."

**Critical**: FY2025 RMB SPV LTV was **59.1%** vs 50.0% covenant — a **9.1pp breach**. Condoned post-year-end; remedied by Portside transfer Jan 2026. FY2026 RMB SPV LTV 26.4% — substantial headroom restored. **Forecast implication**: confirms Portside disposal was covenant-driven, not purely opportunistic; confirms RMB relationship intact. No ICR breach at any SPV (all ≥1.1x covenant). **No ICR waiver exists** — the 1.4x referenced in D009 is not a funder covenant per Note 33.

**Note 34 footnote `*` [D018.10, pp. 284, 286]:**
> "* Current year disclosure was enhanced to split retail and commercial and comparatives have been updated as well."

Changes the headline: FY2025 Level 3 reconciliation comparatives were **re-presented** to split Retail/Commercial. This means FY2025 Retail/Commercial FV movements (Retail +R314,192k; Commercial −R641,728k investment property; Retail −R452,392k; Commercial +R457,942k held-for-sale) are **restated/reconstructed**, not originally disclosed at that granularity. **Forecast implication**: use FY2026 split (Retail −R78,478k; Commercial −R355,414k investment property) as the reliable base; treat FY2025 split with caution.

**Note 34 qualification [D018.10, p. 286]:**
> "There have been no transfers between level 1, level 2 and level 3 during the year. The derivative financial instruments were valued as being the difference between the present value of interest payments at the fixed rate and the projected interest payments based on the forward yield curve. The Company and the Group subsidiaries do not utilise derivatives for speculative purposes other than interest rate risk management."

Confirms all investment property and derivatives are Level 3 / Level 2 respectively; no Level 1 or Level 3 transfers. Derivative valuation is mark-to-market on forward yield curve — **no hedge-ineffectiveness or hedge-accounting detail disclosed here** (carried forward Q260/Q261).

**Note 35 going-concern qualifications [D018.10, pp. 287–288]:**
> "The Group's current liabilities exceed its current assets (including non-current assets held-for-sale) by R2.3 billion. The company's current liabilities of R3.8 billion exceed its current assets by R3.0 billion. The excess of current liabilities over current assets is as a result of the Group's funding facilities maturing at 31 March 2027 and reflected as short-term."

**Critical liquidity qualification**: R2.3bn Group / R3.0bn Company **working-capital deficit** — a material going-concern indicator. Mitigants: (i) facilities mature 31 Mar 2027, extension discussions underway; (ii) disposal pipeline; (iii) rights offer completed; (iv) Board target debt R1.4bn / LTV <40% / ICR 1.6x. **Forecast implication**: the entire debt stack (R2,973m gross) is current — refinancing risk is the single largest forecast variable. If extensions fail, forced-sale risk. Board "acknowledges the uncertainty related to the sale of disposal assets" — a rare explicit qualification.

> "The Board is committed to reduce its debt exposure to an overall debt level of R1,4 billion, LTV of below 40% and an ICR of 1,6 times following the implementation of the strategy."

**Board target**: debt R1.4bn (from R2,973m — a **R1,573m reduction**), LTV <40%, ICR 1.6x. This is the explicit forecast anchor for capital structure.

**Note 36 post-year-end disposals [D018.10, p. 289]:**
> "The net disposal proceeds amount to: The Buzz Shopping Centre – R150,0 million; Waterford – R65,0 million; The Buzz vacant land – R38,8 million; Valleyview – R16,2 million; Edgars Polokwane – R24,1 million. Following these disposals the vacancies reduced from 10,9% to 8,4% and the LTV reduced from 43,3% to 41,1%. A sale agreement was concluded for the disposal of BMW Fourways at a selling price of R174,0 million. Upon transfer of the asset, the LTV will decrease further to 39,6%."

**Critical**: R294.1m net proceeds already transferred; BMW Fourways R174.0m signed but not transferred. LTV path: 43.3% → 41.1% (post R294.1m) → 39.6% (post BMW R174.0m). **Forecast implication**: R468.1m total post-year-end disposal proceeds; LTV reaches Board's <40% target only after BMW transfer. Vacancy 10.9% → 8.4% — a 2.5pp improvement, material for NPI forecast.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Footnote markers `[^4]`, `[^5]`, `[^0]`, `[^6]` on p. 296 (lease expiry by GLA chart)**: The captured evidence contains **footnote markers but no corresponding footnote definitions**. The markers appear embedded in garbled chart text (`50By G[^4],L[^0]%A [^5],[^4]%`, `[^34],[^6]T%o3t4a,l6%`). **The footnote text is missing from this section capture** — I will not fabricate it. A verification question is raised (Q291 below) to locate the definitions in D016/D020. The markers likely relate to the By-GLA lease expiry table's basis (e.g., excluding vacant space, or Fourways Mall 50%-share treatment), which materially affects the 43,9% Fourways Mall GLA concentration figure.

- **Qualification p. 292: "No gradings have been assigned to retail properties and all the commercial properties are A-grade properties."** This is a **material qualification**: the 65,7% A-grade GLA figure on p. 295 **cannot** be a portfolio-wide grading — it must be a **commercial-only or partial** grading, because retail (187 495 m² of 235 922 m² total = **79,5% of GLA**) is ungraded. This **contradicts** the implied portfolio-wide A-grade 65,7% and the "70,2% A-grade by revenue" claim (Q40/Q67). Verification question raised (Q292).

- **Qualification p. 295: "The above vacancy percentages represent the vacant space per sector."** This confirms the vacancy table is **space-based (GLA)**, not revenue- or value-weighted. The **Commercial 45,2%** vacancy is therefore a GLA measure on a **48 427 m²** commercial portfolio (20,5% of total GLA) — high in percentage but smaller in absolute m² than Retail's 11,0% on 187 495 m². This changes the NPI-at-risk weighting: Retail vacancy (11,0% × 187 495 m² ≈ 20 624 m²) is **larger in absolute terms** than Commercial (45,2% × 48 427 m² ≈ 21 889 m²) — roughly comparable. Verification question raised (Q293).

- **Yield table p. 297 — "Average annualised property yield"**: The **Group Commercial yield 14,5% (2025: 8,1%)** is an **extreme outlier** — a near-doubling. Combined with 45,2% Commercial vacancy, this signals either (a) NPI held while value collapsed, or (b) a small commercial NPI base divided by a collapsed value. The **Company Commercial yield 1,9% (2025: 8,1%)** is even more anomalous — a **collapse to 1,9%** — suggesting the Company's commercial NPI is near-zero or the Company holds a different commercial mix. These yields **do not reconcile** to a single cap-rate story and require decomposition. Verification question raised (Q294).

- **Yield table p. 297 — Group vs Company divergence**: Group all-sectors yield **6,5%** vs Company **4,7%**; Group Retail **5,2%** vs Company **5,2%** (tie); Group Commercial **14,5%** vs Company **1,9%**. The **Commercial divergence (14,5% vs 1,9%)** is the single largest Group/Company gap and points to a **structural difference in commercial asset holding** (likely Group holds the distressed/vacant commercial via subsidiaries, Company holds a different or impaired set). Verification question raised (Q295).

- **Escalation table p. 297 — Group 7,0% vs Company 6,6%**: Group escalation **rose** (6,7%→7,0%) while Company escalation was **flat** (6,6%→6,6%). Commercial escalation **rose** (7,4%→7,8% Group; flat 7,0% Company). Retail escalation **flat** (6,5%→6,6% Group; flat 6,5% Company). The **7,0% Group escalation vs 6,0% held-for-sale rental-growth assumption** (Q193) is a **100bp discrepancy** — the portfolio is escalating faster than the valuation assumes, which is **conservative for valuations but positive for NPI forecasting**. Verification question raised (Q296).

- **Lease expiry "By revenue" vs "By GLA" tables (p. 296)**: The two tables give **materially different** expiry profiles — By revenue Mar 30 = 44,5% vs By GLA Mar 30 = 33,9%; By revenue >Mar 30 = 17,2% vs By GLA 25,0%. This means **high-revenue tenants expire earlier** (Mar 30 revenue-weighted 44,5% > GLA-weighted 33,9%) while **low-revenue tenants expire later** (>Mar 30 GLA 25,0% > revenue 17,2%). This is a **negative reversion signal** — the near-term expiry cliff is revenue-concentrated. Verification question raised (Q297).

- **Fourways Mall concentration (p. 292, p. 296)**: Fourways Mall (50%) is **90 242 m² = 38,3% of total GLA** and **40,8% of revenue** (By revenue) / **43,9% of GLA** (By GLA). This is **extreme single-asset concentration** for a REIT. Combined with the lowest-tier retail rental (R177,87/m²) and the NPI collapse (Q137), this is the **dominant forecast risk**. Verification question raised (Q298).

REIT Disclosures
The third edition of the SA REIT Association’s best practice recommendations was issued in February 2026 (2026 SA REIT 
BPRs) and is effective for reporting periods commencing on or after 1 January 2020. All information in the tables disclosed 
below are derived from the audited annual financial statements as disclosed in the 2026 Integrated Report.
The SA REIT ratios include the calculation of SA REIT Funds from Operations (FFO), Funds from operations per share (FFOPS) and 
other Pro-forma information (collectively referred to as “Pro-forma Financial Information”). Pro-forma Financial Information 
constitutes Pro-forma measures and is pro forma financial information in terms of the JSE Listings Requirements.
Basis of preparation: Non-IFRS Financial information
The Pro-forma Financial Information has been compiled to provide investors with performance metrics that are commonly 
used in the industry to enable direct comparison of South African Real Estate Investment Trusts. Due to its nature the Pro￾forma Financial Information may not fairly present the results of operations of the Group and Company.
The Directors are responsible for compiling the Pro-forma Financial Information on the basis of the Applicable Criteria 
specified in the JSE Listings Requirements and the Guide on Pro forma Financial Information, issued by SAICA. To the Director’s 
best knowledge and belief, no facts have been omitted or untrue statements made that would make the tables provided be 
regarded as false or misleading.
The Pro-forma Financial Information has been prepared for illustrative purposes only and, because of its nature, may not 
fairly represent the Group’s financial position, changes in equity, results from operations and cash flows. The underlying 
information used in the preparation of the Pro-forma Financial Information has been prepared using the accounting policies 
in place for the period ended 31 March 2026.
The information provided has not been reviewed or reported on by Accelerate’s auditors. Notwithstanding that the 
information is presented as unaudited, all the information is derived directly from the audited annual financial statements 
as at 31 March 2026. Accordingly, assurance has been placed on the published audited annual financial statements, with 
direct cross-referencing to the audited information per the annual financial statements. For the avoidance of doubt, an 
independent reporting accountant’s assurance report on the Pro-forma Financial Information presented as at 31 March 2025 
was obtained and is available on the Group’s website at https://www.acceleratepf.co.za/investorcentre/#AssuranceReport

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

- **Q267 (High) — R300,000k restatement of trade and other payables; confirm FY2026 derecognition credit excluded from distributable earnings.**
  - **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D012/D018)`
  - **Answer & evidence**: The SA REIT FFO bridge explicitly deducts the R300,000k derecognition credit as a non-distributable "Gains or losses on the modification of financial instruments" adjustment [D020, p. 300]. This confirms the credit is excluded from SA REIT FFO. The D012 comparative restatement and the explicit SA REIT distributable-earnings (post company-specific adjustments) exclusion remain open.

- **Q225 / Q241 (High) — VAT refund R84,247k and insurance R82,500k excluded from distributable earnings.**
  - **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D018)`
  - **Answer & evidence**: Neither the R84,247k VAT refund nor the R82,500k insurance claim appears as a separate line in the SA REIT FFO bridge [D020, p. 300]; both sit inside "Profit or loss per IFRS" and are not added back, implying they remain in FFO unless captured in "Other deductible items not distributed" (which is nil in FY2026). This is a tension: if these are one-off non-operating items, their retention in FFO inflates FFO by ~R166.7m. Explicit exclusion treatment still to be confirmed in D018/D004.

- **Q239 (High) — R300,000k non-cash derecognition credit excluded from distributable earnings and FFO.**
  - **Status**: `Resolved (for FFO)`
  - **Answer & evidence**: Confirmed deducted in the FFO bridge [D020, p. 300]. FFO therefore excludes the R300,000k credit.

- **Q240 / Q277 (High) — Three-way FV loss discrepancy (Note 22 R423,412k vs Note 29 R428,888k vs Note 34 R433,892k).**
  - **Status**: `Partially resolved (remainder stays open for D018)`
  - **Answer & evidence**: The SA REIT FFO bridge uses R423,412k total FV loss, split into investment property R428,888k and debt/equity instruments FV gain of (R5,476k) [D020, p. 300]. This confirms the R423,412k = R428,888k − R5,476k arithmetic. The Note 34 R433,892k third figure remains unreconciled.

- **Q244 / Q245 (High) — Weighted average shares restated for IAS 33 bonus factor; shares in issue vs treasury.**

This differs from Note 29 weighted average 1,970,950,395 and shares in issue 2,045,868,398 gross of treasury 44,829,303. The 2,045,495k figure implies treasury of 373k (2,045,868 − 2,045,495), not 44,829k — a material reconciliation gap (~44.5m shares) that must be resolved.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Basis of preparation qualification [D020, p. 298]**: The SA REIT BPRs are stated as "third edition… issued February 2026… effective for reporting periods commencing on or after 1 January 2020." This is internally inconsistent (a 2026 edition cannot be effective from 2020) and suggests boilerplate carry-over. More importantly, the Pro-forma Financial Information is explicitly **"not reviewed or reported on by Accelerate's auditors"** and is **"unaudited"** — only the underlying AFS carry assurance. This means every SA REIT ratio in D020 (LTV, FFO, NAV, vacancy, cost-to-income, ICR, WACD) is unaudited and must be independently recomputed from D012–D018 before use in the forecast. The FY2025 comparative had an independent reporting accountant's assurance report (per the note), but FY2026 does not — a downgrade in assurance year-on-year.

- **SA REIT LTV footnote/definition [D020, p. 299]**: Net debt (A) = Gross debt R3,002,017k − cash R110,456k − derivative financial instruments R5,574k = R2,885,987k. Denominator (B) = Total assets R6,843,367k − cash R110,456k − derivative financial instruments R8,764k − trade and other receivables R122,294k = R6,601,853k. **Arithmetic check**: R2,885,987 / R6,601,853 = 43.72% ✓. **Tension**: the derivative deduction in net debt uses R5,574k (net derivative position) while the denominator uses R8,764k (gross derivative asset) — an inconsistent basis that understates net debt by R3,190k (the derivative liability) and overstates the denominator by the same, marginally understating LTV. Immaterial (~5bp) but a methodology flag. Also note LTV improved from 48.3% to 43.7% — driven by gross debt falling R747,187k and total assets falling R1,022,419k; the LTV improvement is therefore partly denominator shrinkage (disposals), not purely deleveraging.

- **SA REIT FFO bridge [D020, p. 300]**:
  - IFRS loss (R45,888k) + accounting adjustments R173,727k + investing adjustments nil + FX/hedging nil + other deductible items nil = FFO R127,839k. **Arithmetic check**: −45,888 + 173,727 = 127,839 ✓.
  - **Critical observation**: "Other deductible items not distributed" is **nil in FY2026** vs (R231,376k) in FY2025. FY2025 contained three non-cash deductions: Headlease income accrual (R61,801k), interest income accrual on related-party balances (R98,512k), and interest expense reversal Rebuilt claim (R71,063k). The FY2026 nil means either these items did not recur (plausible — Headlease and Rebuilt claim were FY2025-specific) or they were not deducted. **This is the single largest driver of the FFO swing from (R71,326k) to R127,839k** — a R199m favourable swing from non-recurrence of these deductions alone, on top of the R300m derecognition add-back. FFO quality is therefore heavily dependent on one-off non-recurrence, not underlying operations.
  - **VAT refund R84,247k and insurance R82,500k are NOT separately deducted** — they remain inside IFRS profit and thus inside FFO. Combined ~R166.7m, this is ~130% of reported FFO of R127.8m. If these are genuinely one-off, underlying recurring FFO is materially negative. **This is the most important forecast risk in D020.**
  - **Asset impairments nil in FY2026** vs R1,046,461k in FY2025 — the FY2025 impairment (largely the R1.05bn trade receivable ECL per Note 10) did not recur. This is the second-largest FFO swing driver.
  - **Straight-lining R49,702k** added back (FY2025: R63,880k) — consistent with Note 26/17.
  - **Depreciation R613k** added back (FY2025: R399k) — consistent with PPE R124k + ROU R489k.
  - **No disposal gains/losses adjustment** — nil in both years, despite R788.5m gross disposals in FY2026. This is a tension: either disposals were at carrying value (unlikely given FV losses) or disposal gains/losses are embedded in IFRS profit and not stripped out. Must verify in D018 Note 22/34.

- **Company-specific adjustments [D020, p. 301]**:
  - Fourways Mall capex requirement (R100.0m) = **(4.89) cents/share** deduction. **Arithmetic check**: R100,000k / 2,045,495k shares = 4.89 cents ✓.
  - Additional capex and costs for disposal properties = **(1.27) cents/share**. Footnote `*`: "Additional capex of R26.0 million is estimated to be spent on assets identified for disposal." **Arithmetic check**: R26,000k / 2,045,495k = 1.27 cents ✓.
  - **Distributable income per share = 0.09 cents** (FY2025: (3.97) cents). **Arithmetic check**: FFOPS 6.25 − 4.89 − 1.27 = 0.09 ✓.
  - **This is the headline finding**: DIPS of 0.09 cents is effectively zero. The entire FFO of 6.25 cps is consumed by R126m of company-specific capex requirements (R100m Fourways Mall + R26m disposal assets). **Any dividend declaration would exceed DIPS** — must check D004/D010 for DPS and payout ratio. If a dividend was declared, it was funded from capital/reserves, not distributable income.

- **SA REIT NAV [D020, p. 301]**: NAV R3,701,003k / 2,045,495k shares = R1.81 (FY2025: R2.03). **Arithmetic check**: 3,701,003 / 2,045,495 = R1.809 ✓. NAV fell 11% despite FFO positive — driven by FV losses (R428,888k) and the R300m derecognition credit being non-cash (no NAV benefit). NAV per share R1.81 vs likely share price — check for NAV discount/premium in D001/D004.

- **SA REIT GLA vacancy [D020, p. 302]**: Vacant GLA 25,631 m² / portfolio GLA 235,922 m² = 10.86% ✓ (rounded 10.9%). Note 1 cross-references Appendix B p. 292 — consistent with D019. **Tension**: portfolio GLA fell from 294,970 m² to 235,922 m² (−20.0%) — consistent with disposals, but the vacancy fell from 57,266 m² to 25,631 m² (−55.2%). The vacancy reduction is disproportionately large vs GLA reduction — implies either (a) vacant space was disproportionately in disposed assets, or (b) letting success. Must reconcile to D019 sub-sector vacancy (Retail 11.0%, Commercial 45.2%).

- **SA REIT cost-to-income ratios [D020, pp. 302–305]**:
  - Gross total CIR 50.7% (2025: 48.3%) — **deteriorated 240bp**. Total costs R369,345k / gross revenue R728,640k = 50.69% ✓.
  - Gross property CIR 41.7% (2025: 40.0%) — **deteriorated 170bp**. Property expenses R303,867k / gross revenue R728,640k = 41.70% ✓.
  - Gross admin CIR 9.1% (2025: 8.4%) — **deteriorated 70bp**. Admin R66,091k / R728,640k = 9.07% ✓.
  - Net total CIR 30.5% (2025: 30.0%) — **deteriorated 50bp**. Net costs R157,939k / rental R517,234k = 30.54% ✓.
  - Net property CIR 17.9% (2025: 18.8%) — **improved 90bp**. Net operating costs R92,461k / R517,234k = 17.88% ✓.
  - Net admin CIR 12.8% (2025: 11.3%) — **deteriorated 150bp**. R66,091k / R517,234k = 12.78% ✓.
  - **Key insight**: Gross ratios deteriorated because gross revenue fell 11.6% (R824,036k → R728,640k) faster than costs fell 7.2% (R397,886k → R369,345k). Net property CIR improved because recoveries fell less than property expenses — but net admin CIR deteriorated sharply because admin costs are largely fixed while rental income fell 15.1%. **Operating leverage is negative** — the cost base is not flexing with the shrinking portfolio. This is a critical forecast input: admin costs ~R66m are near-fixed and will not scale down with further disposals.
  - **Note**: the "Net Administration Cost-To-Income Ratio" label on p. 305 is mislabelled as "gross administration cost-to-income ratio (%) (V/W)" in the table — a labelling error; the ratio 12.8% is correctly net admin (admin/rental).

- **SA REIT Cost of Debt [D020, p. 306]**: Fixed rate 10.2% (2025: 11.2%), derivative impact (0.3%), all-in WACD 9.9% (2025: 10.9%). **Tension**: the "Variable interest-rate borrowings — Floating reference rate plus weighted average margin" line is **blank** — no floating rate or margin disclosed. This means either all debt is fixed (inconsistent with Q260's R500m unhedged) or the disclosure is incomplete. Must verify in D018 Note 23/35. The 100bp WACD reduction is a material forecast input — if it reflects refinancing at lower rates, it is sustainable; if it reflects a shift to shorter-dated cheaper facilities, it may reverse at the 31 Mar 2027 maturity wall.

- **SA REIT ICR [D020, p. 306]**: EBITDA (X) R517,642k / net interest (Y) R390,416k = 1.33x ✓ (rounded 1.3x). **Critical observations**:
  - EBITDA includes "Other income" R167,061k (2025: R5,919k) — a R161m increase. This is where the VAT refund (R84,247k) and insurance (R82,500k) sit. **Stripping these two one-offs, EBITDA would be ~R350.3m and ICR ~0.90x — below 1.0x.** This is the single most important forecast finding: the reported 1.3x ICR is entirely dependent on one-off other income. On a recurring basis the Group may not cover interest.
  - EBITDA deducts "Movement in ECL on trade receivables" R8,101k (2025: R1,046,461k) — the FY2025 figure was the R1.05bn impairment that drove the negative ICR. FY2026 ECL charge is normalised.
  - Net interest R390,416k = interest expense R397,841k − interest income R7,425k. Interest income fell from R103,444k to R7,425k (−92.8%) — consistent with related-party loan repayments (Q268). This structurally raises net interest and depresses ICR going forward.
  - **ICR 1.3x vs SPV covenant 1.1x (Q285)** — headroom is thin (~0.2x). If other income normalises, ICR could breach 1.1x. Must confirm covenant levels and whether other income is included in covenant EBITDA definition.
